This statement established a direct connection between the safety of Iranian civil infrastructure and the lives of U.S. personnel deployed in the Middle East.

Wave 41: Hypersonic Strikes Targeting U.S. Personnel

To enforce Larijani's warning, the IRGC launched Wave 41 of its missile campaign. Unlike previous salvos that focused on logistical facilities, this wave utilized hypersonic missiles specifically programmed to target U.S. troop concentrations and personnel depots.

The strikes were executed without warning, utilizing high-velocity warheads designed to penetrate the terminal air defense networks of U.S. bases. The IRGC declared that the operation was executed "without mercy," marking a shift in target selection from static structures to active combat units.

Tactical Shift: Targeting Troop Concentrations in Three Countries

Wave 41 targeted U.S. personnel staging areas across three regional states:

  • United Arab Emirates: Hypersonic missiles struck U.S. troop concentrations along Sheikh Zayed Road and personnel facilities at Al Dhafra Airbase.
  • Kuwait: Salvos targeted U.S. troop staging areas at Ahmad al-Jaber Airbase.
  • Iraq: Precision strikes hit U.S. mobile bases and tactical personnel centers.

Earlier waves of strikes had resulted in U.S. casualties, with reports citing 6 dead and over 140 wounded. The direct targeting of troop concentrations during Wave 41 is expected to result in higher casualty rates, challenging the safety of U.S. deployments in the Gulf.

The Role of U.S. Strategic Heavy Bombers

The IRGC's decision to target U.S. personnel was a direct response to the coalition's strategic bomber campaign. The U.S. military has shifted away from tactical aircraft like the F-22 and F-35, relying instead on its strategic bomber triad.

B-52, B-1B Lancer, and B-21 Raider bombers have conducted consecutive nights of strikes, dropping heavy ordnance on Iranian military concentrations. This heavy bombardment has caused significant casualties among Iranian ground units, prompting the IRGC to utilize its hypersonic missile inventory to strike U.S. troops in neighboring countries.

Conclusion: The Collapse of Rules of Engagement

The exchange of threats between Trump and Larijani, followed by the Wave 41 hypersonic strikes, demonstrates that the conflict has entered a phase of unrestricted escalation. By targeting civilian electrical grids and troop concentrations, both sides have abandoned the rules of engagement that governed earlier phases.

As U.S. strategic bombers continue their sorties and Iran deploys its hypersonic arsenal, the safety of regional logistics nodes has been compromised. The expansion of the combat zone to include U.S. troop centers in the UAE, Kuwait, and Iraq suggests that the confrontation has transitioned into a regional war of attrition, with high risks for all participants.

item.title: Leaked: Damaged US Tanker Lands at Ben Gurion
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing leaked photos of a damaged US KC-135 at Ben Gurion Airport, the evasion of USS Abraham Lincoln, and the joint US-Israeli air campaign.
item.content:encoded:
Leaked: Damaged US Tanker Lands at Ben Gurion

A series of leaks from Israeli media outlets has exposed the scale of U.S. and Israeli air losses during recent operations in western Iraq. High-resolution photographs showing a damaged U.S. KC-135 Stratotanker at Ben Gurion Airport have contradicted official Pentagon accounts of the engagement. This development, combined with satellite tracking showing evasive maneuvers by the carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, has forced the coalition to plan a massive, preemptive air campaign to suppress regional launch sites.

The Leaked Images: Confirming the Second KC-135 Hit

Although the U.S. Defense Department and CENTCOM officially acknowledged the loss of only one KC-135 Stratotanker—claiming it crashed due to a mechanical issue in a non-hostile zone—leaked images from Ben Gurion Airport tell a different story.

The leaked photographs show the second KC-135, which managed to land in Israel, displaying extensive shrapnel damage. The tail section of the tanker was severely compromised, confirming that the aircraft was hit by fragments from a close-proximity missile explosion. The visual reports confirm that both refueling aircraft were targeted and hit during the engagement over western Iraq.

Tail Damage and Casualty Figures at Ben Gurion

The damage to the tail section of the second KC-135 has permanently disabled the aircraft, removing it from the active inventory. The severity of the shrapnel damage also explains why the pilots activated the international emergency code 7700 during their return flight.

The engagement has resulted in significant U.S. casualties. In addition to the four crew members confirmed dead on the first aircraft (with two others missing and presumed dead), several crew members on the second tanker suffered serious injuries from shrapnel and decompression. At least one Israeli liaison officer was on board the damaged aircraft, coordinating the emergency transit.

USS Abraham Lincoln: Course Deviation and Coordinates Spoofing

The U.S. Navy has faced additional challenges with the carrier USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72). While the Pentagon claimed the Lincoln was operating safely at distance, civilian satellite tracking systems detected a major course correction.

The carrier executed a sharp 256-degree turn, indicating it was executing emergency evasive maneuvers following a threat detection. To mask the carrier's actual position, military planners spoofed coordinates, showing the vessel in Bangladesh. In reality, the carrier is operating at a reduced speed of 20.3 knots, attempting to approach within 250 kilometers of the Gulf under heavy defensive cover.

The Massive Preemptive Strike: Mobilizing Bomber Fleets

To regain the operational initiative and secure the Strait of Hormuz, the U.S. and Israel have prepared a massive night strike campaign. The goal of the operation is to "freeze" regional launch sites before they can execute counter-salvos.

The U.S. has mobilized 15 strategic heavy bombers—including B-52, B-1B, and B-2 Spirits—from RAF Fairford in the United Kingdom. These bombers will coordinate with over 180 combat aircraft launched from Israeli bases and U.S. naval assets, including carrier support from the USS Abraham Lincoln moving via Crete, to deliver a high volume of ordnance.

Suppressing the Launch Sites: The Air Campaign in Lebanon

The preemptive air campaign is designed to suppress launch networks in both Iran and Lebanon. To prevent Hezbollah from launching retaliatory strikes while Iran is being targeted, the coalition has intensified its air strikes in Lebanon, covering waves 40 through 44.

The coalition's ground push into southern Lebanon seeks to force Hezbollah's launch teams back from the border, while the massive air strikes aim to suppress their ability to launch long-range missiles into central Israel. This coordinated pressure is designed to create a temporary fire window for the coalition.

The Joint Command: U.S. and Israeli Air Coordination

The current air campaign in Lebanon is operated under a unified U.S.-Israeli joint command center. U.S. planners are directly involved in targeting and flight coordination, integrating U.S. surveillance assets with Israeli strike wings.

While the Israeli government prefers to frame these operations as domestic defense actions, the involvement of U.S. personnel and command systems is extensive. This joint command structure ensures that U.S. refueling tankers and strategic bombers are integrated directly into the targeting loop, seeking to maximize the efficiency of the strikes.

Conclusion: The Race to Prevent Regional Counter-Salvos

The leaks showing the damaged KC-135 at Ben Gurion Airport and the course correction of the USS Abraham Lincoln demonstrate the vulnerabilities of coalition assets. By targeting refueling tankers and carriers, regional forces have degraded the logistics of the air campaign.

As the coalition prepares its 15-bomber strike fleet, the success of the campaign will depend on whether it can neutralize the launch sites before counter-salvos are initiated. The failure of previous strikes to prevent launches suggests that the preemptive campaign carries a high risk of retaliation, shaping the final phases of the confrontation.

item.title: Failed Raid: Hezbollah Shoots Down Israeli Chopper
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing Israel's failed 15-helicopter commando raid in eastern Lebanon, the downing of a chopper, and joint Iranian-Lebanese retaliatory strikes.
item.content:encoded:
Failed Raid: Hezbollah Shoots Down Israeli Chopper

In a significant tactical escalation, Hezbollah forces successfully repelled a massive Israeli heliborne commando operation in eastern Lebanon. The infiltration, which involved a fleet of 15 helicopters, ended in disaster for the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) after Hezbollah fighters managed to shoot down one of the aircraft. This failed raid highlights the resilience of Hezbollah’s air defense and tactical networks.

The 15-Helicopter Infiltration and Shootdown

According to reports from Agence France-Presse (AFP) and Lebanese security sources, the Israeli operation began around midnight on Monday. A fleet of 15 Israeli helicopters crossed into Lebanese airspace from the Syrian border direction.

The helicopters flew over Yahfoufa, Nabi Chit, Arsal, and Ras Baalbek. As they attempted to insert elite infantry units in the Serghaya plain near the border, Hezbollah forces detected the movement. Utilizing anti-aircraft weaponry and heavy machine guns, the fighters engaged the aircraft directly, striking and downing one Israeli helicopter, forcing a chaotic halt to the infiltration.

Heavy Clashes on the Eastern Mountain Chain

Following the downing of the helicopter, intense infantry clashes erupted on the eastern mountain chain (Al-Silsila al-Sharqiya). The fighting concentrated in the rugged Jaroud Nabi Chit and Sha'ra areas, where Israeli special forces tried to establish a foothold and rescue stranded personnel.

Hezbollah deployed artillery, mortars, and anti-tank guided missiles (ATGMs) to pin down the landed troops. The rugged terrain turned into a fierce battleground as Lebanese security sources confirmed that the Israeli commando team failed to achieve any of its tactical objectives and was forced to withdraw under heavy fire.

The "Ron Arad" Pretext and Family Backlash

This failed landing marks the second Israeli commando operation in Nabi Chit within a few days. The previous Friday, a similar raid was exposed, forcing the Israeli Air Force to conduct a massive "fire belt" of 40 airstrikes to secure the retreat of their trapped special forces.

The Israeli military claimed these high-risk operations were aimed at locating relics or intelligence regarding the long-lost navigator Ron Arad, who disappeared in Lebanon in 1986. However, this pretext has faced heavy criticism inside Israel. Arad's family questioned the wisdom of these missions, arguing that putting living soldiers' lives at risk to retrieve bones is unnecessary, as we analyzed and quoted her Hebrew statement in a previous article.

Failure of Israel’s Degradation & Unilateral Ceasefire Narratives

The double failure of these commando raids exposes the limits of Israel's military strategy. Tel Aviv has consistently claimed that its campaign has degraded Hezbollah, claiming over 500 fighters killed and thousands of targets destroyed.

However, the rapid redeployment and high readiness of Hezbollah's units tell a different story. In areas like Aitaroun and Lailat al-Adaysseh, Hezbollah has repeatedly repelled Israeli advances, demonstrating that its command structure, communication links, and defensive lines remain intact despite months of intense bombardment.

The Haifa Refinery Strikes: Joint Lebanese-Iranian Firepower

In retaliation for the civilian casualties caused by Israel's airstrikes, a coordinated Lebanese-Iranian missile strike targeted industrial infrastructure in northern Israel. Heavy missiles struck key installations in the Haifa district.

The attack utilized advanced Iranian ballistic missiles, including the Khaibar Shekan and Emad, alongside heavy rocket fire from southern Lebanon. The primary target was the Haifa oil refinery complex. The successful penetration of Israel's air defense network by these heavy missiles caused significant fires and structural damage, demonstrating a unified front.

Geographical Deterrence & Netanyahu’s Security Emergency

The combination of successful air defense operations and heavy missile strikes in the north is establishing a new geographical reality. The Israeli government is facing growing domestic pressure to evacuate more northern settlements due to the threat of drone and rocket attacks.

This has created a direct crisis for Benjamin Netanyahu. The threat of Hezbollah drones reaching the Prime Minister's residence has become a confirmed reality. In response, security protocols for Netanyahu and his cabinet ministers have been heavily reinforced, with new physical barriers and electronic warfare systems deployed around government offices.

Conclusion: A Turning Point in Regional Deterrence

The downing of an Israeli helicopter during a large-scale commando raid marks a turning point in the conflict. It collapses the unilateral interpretation of the security parameters that Israel attempted to impose on Lebanon.

By showing that it can defend its airspace and borders against elite heliborne operations, Hezbollah has reinforced its deterrence posture. As long as Israel continues to violate Lebanese sovereignty, the joint missile and drone capabilities of the resistance axis will continue to challenge the IDF's freedom of action, forcing Tel Aviv to reconsider its strategic options.

item.title: Mojtaba Khamenei's Doctrine: Retaliation & Compensation
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing Mojtaba Khamenei's first address, establishing the two pillars of full retaliation and compensation, and his warning to regional states hosting US bases.
item.content:encoded:
Mojtaba Khamenei's Doctrine: Retaliation & Compensation

In his first official address to the nation, Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei—the designated successor to Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei—has outlined a major shift in Iran's military and diplomatic doctrine. Moving beyond the limited containment strategies that characterized the previous 12-day war, the new leadership has established two unyielding pillars for ending the conflict: "Full Retaliation" (الانتقام الكامل) and "Full Compensation" (التعويض الكامل). This address establishes a new framework for any future ceasefire negotiations.

Mojtaba Khamenei's First Address: Setting a New Tone

The public address by Mojtaba Khamenei represents his formal entry into the strategic decision-making process. The speech focused on defining the long-term parameters of the confrontation with the U.S. and Israel, projecting ideological and military resolve.

A notable feature of the address was the focus on the "Zionist Fitnah" (الفتنة الصهيونية) as the primary driver of the conflict. By framing U.S. President Donald Trump as "seduced" or "infatuated" (مفتون) by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's actions, Mojtaba left room for diplomatic and financial settlements with Washington, while holding Israel responsible for initiating the instability.

The Doctrine of Full Retaliation: No Citizens Left Behind

The first pillar of the new doctrine is the concept of Full Retaliation. Mojtaba Khamenei declared that Iran's response will not be limited to symbolic strikes or targeting specific commanders. Instead, every Iranian citizen who falls victim to coalition strikes constitutes an independent file of retaliation.

He stated: "We will not abandon the revenge for the blood of your martyrs. The retaliation we mean does not stop at commanders; every individual citizen who falls at the hands of the enemy constitutes an independent case in the file of revenge, which remains open until it is fully resolved."

The Doctrine of Full Compensation: A New Sovereign Demand

The second pillar of the doctrine is the demand for Full Compensation. This represents a significant departure from Ali Khamenei's previous approach, where financial compensation was never presented as a primary war aim.

President Masoud Pezeshkian has integrated this demand into diplomatic communications, presenting it to Russian mediators as a key condition for any ceasefire. Under this doctrine, the U.S. and its partners must pay full state-level reparations for all physical, industrial, and human damage caused by their military campaign, including the civilian casualties in Minab and the girls of Tayyebat.

Enforcement Through Destruction: The Seizure of Assets

The new doctrine establishes clear enforcement mechanisms if the U.S. and Israel refuse to pay reparations. Mojtaba Khamenei warned that Iran will utilize asymmetric means to extract what it is owed.

He stated: "We will demand that the enemy pay compensation. If they refuse, we will seize their assets to the extent we deem appropriate. If that is not possible, we will systematically destroy equivalent assets of theirs." This policy directly links the destruction of Iranian infrastructure to reciprocal strikes against U.S. and Israeli logistical, financial, and maritime assets in the region.

The U.S. Humanitarian Compensation Strategy and Minab

In response to the demand for reparations, the U.S. intelligence community has suggested a alternative framework. To avoid establishing a precedent of paying state-level war reparations, U.S. planners have proposed direct humanitarian payouts to victims' families, specifically targeting the families of the Minab school strike.

The Iranian leadership has rejected this proposal, viewing it as an attempt to bypass state accountability. Tehran insists that all compensation must be paid directly to the state treasury as formal reparations, ensuring that the U.S. administration accepts legal responsibility for the consequences of its campaign.

Advice to Regional States Hosting U.S. Bases

Mojtaba Khamenei addressed neighboring countries hosting U.S. military installations, advising them to shut down these bases to protect their own security. However, he framed this as "advice" (نصيحة) rather than an ultimatum.

He introduced a new jurisprudential decree: if regional governments publicly condemn the U.S.-Israeli strikes and deny them political legitimacy, Iran will treat the U.S. use of their territory as "forced utilization" (استغلال قسري). Under this decree, Iran will not hold host nations responsible or target their domestic assets, reserving its strikes strictly for the U.S. military components.

Conclusion: The Transition from Containment to Deterrence

The first address by Mojtaba Khamenei outlines a new strategic reality for the Middle East. By establishing full retaliation and compensation as conditions for peace, the new leadership has raised the stakes for the U.S. and Israel.

The warning that Iran will seize or destroy equivalent assets if compensation is denied suggests that the conflict will remain volatile even during ceasefire negotiations. As regional states assess their position regarding U.S. bases, the new doctrine will shape the diplomatic and military dynamics, signaling that Tehran is prepared for a long-term confrontation to protect its sovereign interests.

item.title: Blinded Eyes: US Radar Struck, Warning Times Reduced
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing Israel's admission of the destruction of the US AN/TPY-2 radar at Site 512 in the Negev, reducing civilian missile warning times.
item.content:encoded:
Blinded Eyes: US Radar Struck, Warning Times Reduced

In a significant admission, Israeli military censors have permitted the publication of reports confirming the destruction of a vital U.S. early-warning radar in the Negev Desert. The facility, known as Site 512, was targeted by a precision Iranian missile strike. The loss of this advanced sensor has directly impacted regional air defenses, leading to a drastic reduction in warning times for incoming missile threats across Israel.

The Acknowledgment: Confirming the Site 512 Radar Hit

For the first time, Israeli Hebrew media, including Channel 12, has acknowledged that a precision strike by Iranian forces targeted and disabled the early-warning radar at U.S. Site 512. The facility is located on Mount Har Qeren (جبل جرن) in the Negev Desert, approximately 20 kilometers from Gaza and 30 kilometers southwest of Beersheba.

Although Israeli officials previously downplayed the site's significance by claiming it primarily serves U.S. strategic interests, the acknowledgment of the strike highlights the connection between the facility and Israel's domestic air defense network.

The Role of the AN/TPY-2 Radar in Israel's Defense

The disabled system is the AN/TPY-2, a high-performance, mobile X-band radar developed by Raytheon, costing approximately $300 million. This system serves as the primary sensor for the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missile defense network.

The role of the AN/TPY-2 is to detect, track, and classify long-range ballistic missiles launched from Iran or its regional allies. Because of its high resolution and long range, it provides early-warning tracking data directly to both U.S. and Israeli air defense batteries, allowing interceptors to be calculated and launched early in the threat's flight path.

Why Warning Times Have Been Drastically Reduced

The destruction of the AN/TPY-2 radar has created a critical gap in early-warning coverage. Without the long-range tracking data provided by Site 512, local air defense systems must rely on shorter-range sensors, which detect incoming missiles much later in their flight.

This reduction in early tracking capability has directly translated into a shorter warning window for Israeli civilians. The home front command has had to adjust warning protocols, leaving civilians with significantly less time to seek shelter after sirens are activated, explaining why warnings have become shorter and less predictable.

Khatam al-Anbiya HQ's Coordinated Strike on Five U.S. Bases

According to official declarations from Iran’s Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, the hit on Site 512 was part of a coordinated operation targeting five strategic U.S. bases in the region. The strikes combined precision ballistic missiles and suicide drone swarms.

Alongside the radar complex in the Negev Desert, the operation targeted U.S. troop concentrations and logistics depots at Camp Arifjan in Kuwait. The coordinated nature of the strikes demonstrated the ability of Iranian planners to execute simultaneous actions against regional logistics nodes.

Non-Conventional U.S. Airstrikes and Iran's Warhead Standardization

The escalation has occurred alongside a U.S. heavy bomber campaign targeting Iranian infrastructure. U.S. forces have conducted intensive strikes using B-1B Lancer and B-2 Spirit bombers, striking thousands of civilian and industrial targets to degrade Iran's economic capacity.

In response to this campaign, Iranian commanders have adjusted their missile doctrine. The IRGC has ceased deploying warheads weighing under one ton (1,000 kilograms) for strategic strikes, standardizing on heavier payloads to maximize the destructive impact on coalition bases and key infrastructure hubs.

Air Defense Deficits: Shifting Patriot Batteries from East Asia

The systematic destruction of air defense assets in the Middle East—including 11 radar systems over the past weeks—has created an urgent demand for replacement components. To cover these gaps, the U.S. military has had to redeploy Patriot batteries from East Asian theatres.

Patriot systems have been moved from South Korea and Japan to the Persian Gulf to protect key bases and shipping lanes. This redeployment has reduced the air defense coverage available in East Asia, leaving regional allies with limited coverage as the Pentagon prioritizes the Middle East theater.

Conclusion: The Vulnerability of Regional Defense Networks

The neutralization of the AN/TPY-2 radar at Site 512 highlights the vulnerability of centralized early-warning nodes. By targeting the sensor array of the THAAD system, Iranian forces bypassed the interceptor batteries, degrading the entire defense network.

The reduction in warning times for civilians and the redeployment of air defense assets from other global theaters indicate that the conflict is straining coalition resources. As long as these key radar and communication hubs remain out of service, the effectiveness of regional air defenses will remain degraded, shaping the tactical calculations of both sides.

item.title: AI Warfare: The Biometric Hunt for Netanyahu and Mojtaba
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing the AI biometric warfare standoff between Israel and Iran, Netanyahu's Star Cafe video controversy, and Mojtaba Khamenei's isolation.
item.content:encoded:
AI Warfare: The Biometric Hunt for Netanyahu and Mojtaba

The conflict between Israel and Iran has entered a phase of biometric warfare, with both nations utilizing advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) to track and target high-value leaders. To prevent predictive AI models and drone guidance networks from mapping their locations, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Iran’s Mojtaba Khamenei have adopted strict non-appearance protocols. Any visual or audio releases must undergo digital processing to prevent adversaries from reconstructing raw biometric profiles.

Algorithm Safety: The Silent Battle of AI Tracking

The intelligence agencies of Israel and the United States are locked in a struggle with Iranian cyber units over "Algorithm Safety" (أمن الخوارزميات). Modern tracking systems do not rely solely on physical satellite tracking; instead, they integrate AI algorithms capable of analyzing minor details in public media releases.

By feeding raw audio and video clips into neural networks, analysts can build predictive behavioral models. These models analyze vocal micro-stressors, facial micro-expressions, and background reflections to estimate a subject's location, health, and schedule, making the release of raw media highly risky.

The Risk of Raw Footprints: Biometric Vulnerability

For leadership targets like Benjamin Netanyahu and Mojtaba Khamenei, releasing un-processed media represents a direct security threat. A single raw recording allows enemy AI systems to extract:

  • Vocal Signatures: Revealing emotional state, physical condition, and biometric indicators.
  • Environmental Cues: Reconstructing ambient lighting, acoustics, and background reflections to pinpoint coordinates.
  • Physical Micro-movements: Tracking gait and posture to build target recognition files for autonomous drones.

To counter this, both leaders require all media releases to undergo digital modifications, such as adding subtitles or watermark overlays, to disrupt the tracking capacity of tracking algorithms.

Netanyahu’s Star Cafe Appearance in the Jerusalem Hills

To counter widespread social media rumors claiming he was killed in an Iranian missile strike, Netanyahu's office released a brief visual clip showing him visiting the "Star Cafe" in the Jerusalem hills. The cafe is owned by IDF reservists, a commercial detail promoted in cooperation with Keshet 12 and comedian Hanoch Daum.

While the clip aimed to show Netanyahu in a calm environment, it was designed with security precautions. The surrounding area was placed under tight security, and the clip itself was processed to prevent real-time telemetry extraction by foreign intelligence.

The Digital Backlash: Star Cafe Targeted on Google Maps

Netanyahu's visit to the Star Cafe triggered a digital campaign. Pro-Palestinian, Iranian, and Turkish internet users flooded the cafe’s Google Maps profile with thousands of negative reviews and low ratings, criticizing the prime minister.

According to reports in the Israeli newspaper Maariv, the business owners are considering legal action against users who manipulated the ratings to damage the establishment's commercial standing. The campaign shows how physical leadership movements can lead to digital disruptions for local businesses.

Visual Integrity Debated: Matt Wallace’s Analysis on X

The released clip of Netanyahu at the cafe sparked skepticism online. Visual content creator Matt Wallace analyzed the clip on X, slowing down the footage to identify potential anomalies.

Wallace pointed to specific details, including a visual glitch near Netanyahu's coat pocket, the physics of the coffee movement, and a masked individual in the background. While some accounts claimed the clip was entirely AI-generated, analysts conclude the clip was authentic but intentionally processed with digital filters to alter biometric signatures and prevent tracking algorithms from mapping the scene.

Mojtaba Khamenei: Absolute Isolation Under AI Watch

In Iran, Mojtaba Khamenei—who is coordinating IRGC operations and positioning himself as the successor after the death of Ali Khamenei—faces similar security constraints. Western intelligence has circulated rumors that Mojtaba is dead or receiving medical treatment in Moscow, attempting to bait him into making a public appearance.

Iranian security services understand that a raw video or audio release would allow U.S. and Israeli AI systems to track him using integrated city cameras and acoustic sensors. Consequently, Mojtaba remains in absolute isolation, communicating solely through verified, processed messages.

Conclusion: The Non-Appearance Protocol as Strategic Defense

The biometric standoff between Netanyahu and Mojtaba Khamenei shows that visibility has become a vulnerability. By using AI to analyze vocal and visual data, both sides have turned public appearances into targeting vectors.

As intelligence agencies attempt to track these leaders, the reliance on processed media will continue. The necessity of modifying every release to disrupt AI tracking indicates that the conflict is fought not only with physical weapons, but also in the digital space, where biometric safety is essential for survival.

item.title: Oil Surges Past $110: Trump Freezes Iranian Energy Strikes
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing Trump's freeze on Iranian energy strikes as oil surpasses $110, Iran's target bank update, and Venezuela's hardline pivot.
item.content:encoded:
Oil Surges Past $110: Trump Freezes Iranian Energy Strikes

U.S. President Donald Trump has ordered a freeze on air strikes targeting Iran's energy infrastructure. According to The Wall Street Journal, citing Pentagon and Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) sources, the decision follows a sharp increase in global oil prices, which surged past $110 per barrel. The freeze occurs as Iran warns Gulf nations of retaliatory strikes on their refineries and updates its target list, while Venezuela adjusts its defense leadership to prepare for a prolonged standoff with Washington.

The Freeze: WSJ Outlines Trump’s Energy Halt

The freeze on strikes targeting Iranian gas and oil fields was prompted by rising economic costs. The Wall Street Journal reported that the Pentagon advised Trump that continued bombardment of Iranian energy assets would lead to a global energy supply crisis.

Trump had approved the initial strikes on the South Pars field to gain leverage over Tehran and demonstrate control over global energy markets. However, the immediate Iranian counter-strikes on Gulf shipping and oil infrastructure forced Washington to halt the campaign to prevent further market disruption.

Oil Surges Past $110: The Shockwave on Wall Street

Following the mutual strikes on energy facilities in Iran and the Gulf, global energy markets reacted immediately. The price of Brent crude oil rose to $106 per barrel, and then quickly surpassed $110.

This surge has affected the U.S. economy, raising domestic fuel costs and feeding inflation. For Trump, who made low energy prices a cornerstone of his economic policy, the market reaction showed that a prolonged conflict with Iran would lead to domestic economic disruption, undermining his political standing.

Updating the Target Bank: Iran’s Warning to Gulf Allies

As part of its deterrence strategy, Tehran has updated its military target list, warning citizens of Gulf states to stay away from domestic energy facilities. The updated list covers key infrastructure across the region:

  • Saudi Arabia: The Ras Tanura, Sasref, Samref, and Jazan refineries.
  • United Arab Emirates: The Ruwais refinery complex.
  • Kuwait: The Al-Zour, Mina Abdulla, and Mina Al-Ahmadi refineries.
  • Bahrain: The Bapco refinery.
  • Israel: The Ashdod and Haifa refineries (with Haifa already sustaining damage).

Mapping the Red Lines: The Strike on Ras Laffan

The seriousness of Iran's warnings was demonstrated by a missile strike targeting Qatar's Ras Laffan refinery. The IRGC launched five precision missiles at the facility; while regional air defenses intercepted four, the fifth warhead struck the refinery compound.

This strike served as a warning to Gulf capitals. By demonstrating its ability to hit Ras Laffan, Iran showed that Qatar's gas export infrastructure is vulnerable. The message to Doha and Riyadh is clear: if Iranian energy exports are halted by U.S. strikes, Gulf exports will face the same fate.

The Financial Fallout: Fed Warning and Stocks Decline

The energy market disruption has affected U.S. financial markets. Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell kept interest rates unchanged, citing concerns that rising oil prices could trigger a new wave of inflation.

Powell's statements led to a decline in U.S. stock indices as investors adjusted to the prospect of sustained high interest rates. To manage market volatility, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) approved a Nasdaq plan for tokenized securities, showing the pressure on financial institutions to find stabilizing mechanisms during the crisis.

The Venezuelan Front: Hardline Shifts in the Caribbean

The geopolitical crisis has also escalated in the Caribbean. Following the failure of Russian forces under Vladimir Badrinov (Vladimir Putin's successor) to protect Nicolás Maduro's administration from U.S. special operations pressure, Venezuela’s leadership took steps to prepare for conflict.

Despite a $5.2 billion transaction involving the delivery of 10 million barrels of oil to the U.S. in exchange for sanctions relief, Washington continued its military build-up. In response, Venezuela’s Vice President replaced the Defense Minister with a hardline military figure, preparing the nation for a prolonged defense and raising the risk of a new conflict in the Caribbean.

Conclusion: The Limits of U.S. Energy Domination

The freeze on strikes targeting Iranian energy infrastructure shows the limits of the U.S. "energy war" strategy. By demonstrating that it can retaliate against Gulf refineries and disrupt global oil prices, Iran has established a level of deterrence.

As Trump evaluates his options and oil prices remain above $110, the limits of U.S. policy are visible. The inability of U.S. and regional air defenses to protect static installations like Ras Laffan suggests that continuing the air campaign will carry high economic costs, forcing Washington to reconsider its regional objectives.

item.title: True Promise 4: The Collapse of Oil Diplomacy
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing the failure of the Trump-Putin initiative, the start of Iran's True Promise 4 operation, and the deployment of one-ton precision warheads.
item.content:encoded:
True Promise 4: The Collapse of Oil Diplomacy

Following the failure of the backchannel diplomatic initiative mediated by Moscow, the military confrontation in the Middle East has entered its most intense phase. The collapse of the proposed Trump-Putin agreement, which sought to trade diplomatic concessions in Ukraine for oil price stabilization and mediation with Iran, has removed all political constraints. Iran has responded by launching "Operation True Promise 4" (الوعد الصادق 4), utilizing a new generation of high-precision heavy ballistic missiles.

The Collapse of the Trump-Putin Ceasefire Initiative

The diplomatic framework proposed by the U.S. and Russian administrations fell apart after key stakeholders in Tehran and Kyiv rejected the terms of the trade-off. The initiative sought to freeze the conflict in Ukraine while offering concessions to Russia, in exchange for Russian assistance in stabilizing global oil prices and bringing Iran to the negotiating table.

Tehran viewed the terms as an attempt to restrict its defensive options without addressing core security concerns, while Ukraine opposed freezing its borders under Russian control. The collapse of these negotiations has left both the U.S. and Iran committed to resolving their strategic differences on the battlefield.

Heavy Bomber Strikes and Non-Conventional Escalation

Immediately following the failure of the diplomatic initiative, U.S. and Israeli forces launched a massive wave of airstrikes targeting Iranian military installations and civilian infrastructure. The coalition deployed its full strategic bomber fleet, including B-1B Lancer, B-2 Spirit, and next-generation B-21 Raider aircraft operating from British bases.

Simultaneously, the Israeli military deployed heavy surface-to-surface ballistic systems, including Jericho (أريحا) missiles launched from bases near Bnei Brak, east of Tel Aviv. These heavy strikes were supported by U.S. HIMARS rocket systems positioned in the Persian Gulf, aiming to sever Iran's command links.

Operation True Promise 4: The Strategic Targets

Iran's response, code-named Operation True Promise 4, involved launching waves 34 and 35 of ballistic missiles and suicide drones. The operation targeted critical U.S. and Israeli military assets in the region:

  • U.S. Bases: Heavy missile salvos struck the U.S. Fifth Fleet headquarters at Juffair Naval Base in Bahrain and air facilities at Al Dhafra Airbase in the UAE.
  • Northern Israel: Targets included Ramat David Airbase, Haifa Civil Airport, and the military surveillance center in Haifa that processes spy satellite data.
  • Infrastructure: Suicide drones and ballistic missiles targeted Haifa's oil refineries and fuel storage facilities in response to strikes on Iranian oil assets.

The "Noghtavi" Precision Doctrine: One-Ton Warheads

A key feature of Operation True Promise 4 is the deployment of "Noghtavi" (point-target/نقطوي) precision-guided missiles. This term, derived from the Persian word for "point," refers to guidance systems capable of hitting a specific target with surgical accuracy.

These missiles feature a Circular Error Probable (CEP) of less than five meters. This accuracy eliminates the need for area-saturation tactics, allowing single missiles to destroy hardened structures. During this operation, Iran deployed these precision guidance packages on warheads weighing more than one ton (1,000 kilograms), delivering high explosive yields directly onto high-value targets.

Upgraded Ballistic Systems: Khorramshahr-4 and Solid-Fuel Haj Qasem

The missile salvos utilized several of Iran's most advanced ballistic systems:

  • Khorramshahr-4 (خرمشهر 4): A heavy liquid-fueled missile with a range of 2,000 kilometers, carrying a guided warhead exceeding one ton.
  • Haj Qasem (حاج قاسم): Iran's first solid-fuel precision ballistic missile, featuring a range of 1,400 kilometers and an upgraded, highly destructive warhead.
  • Fattah and Kheibar: Hypersonic and precision-guided variants (including the Fattah system operated by Hezbollah) were deployed to penetrate Israel's terminal air defense networks.
  • Emad and Qadr: Upgraded 2026 variants equipped with maneuverable re-entry vehicles (MaRVs) featuring aerodynamic fins, enabling them to execute evasive maneuvers during the final phase of flight.

Countering the "No Military Power Remaining" Narrative

The scale of Operation True Promise 4 directly challenges the U.S. administration's public narrative. In a phone interview with CNBC news, Donald Trump claimed that the military campaign had effectively ended Iran's combat capabilities, stating that they had "no navy, no communications, no air force, and their missiles were scattered and destroyed."

By executing coordinated strikes across multiple countries on day 11 of the escalation, Iran demonstrated that its strategic command remains intact. The IRGC confirmed it retains full control over the Strait of Hormuz, challenging U.S. claims and warning that any attempt to escort oil tankers through the strait would be met with direct force.

Conclusion: The Horizon of Unrestricted Regional Warfare

The failure of the Trump-Putin diplomatic initiative and the launch of Operation True Promise 4 marks a significant escalation in the conflict. By deploying one-ton precision warheads against U.S. and Israeli installations, Iran has shown it can sustain high-intensity operations despite heavy bombardment.

As the U.S. and Israel continue their strategic bomber campaign, the lack of political constraints increases the risk of a wider regional conflict. The reliance on advanced ballistic guidance, heavy payloads, and coordinated coalition actions suggests that both sides are prepared for a long-term confrontation, changing the security dynamics of the Middle East.

Simultaneously, the Israeli military deployed heavy surface-to-surface ballistic systems, including Jericho (أريحا) missiles launched from bases near Bnei Brak, east of Tel Aviv. These heavy strikes were supported by U.S. HIMARS rocket systems positioned in the Persian Gulf, aiming to sever Iran's command links.

Operation True Promise 4: The Strategic Targets

Iran's response, code-named Operation True Promise 4, involved launching waves 34 and 35 of ballistic missiles and suicide drones. The operation targeted critical U.S. and Israeli military assets in the region:

  • U.S. Bases: Heavy missile salvos struck the U.S. Fifth Fleet headquarters at Juffair Naval Base in Bahrain and air facilities at Al Dhafra Airbase in the UAE.
  • Northern Israel: Targets included Ramat David Airbase, Haifa Civil Airport, and the military surveillance center in Haifa that processes spy satellite data.
  • Infrastructure: Suicide drones and ballistic missiles targeted Haifa's oil refineries and fuel storage facilities in response to strikes on Iranian oil assets.

The "Noghtavi" Precision Doctrine: One-Ton Warheads

A key feature of Operation True Promise 4 is the deployment of "Noghtavi" (point-target/نقطوي) precision-guided missiles. This term, derived from the Persian word for "point," refers to guidance systems capable of hitting a specific target with surgical accuracy.

These missiles feature a Circular Error Probable (CEP) of less than five meters. This accuracy eliminates the need for area-saturation tactics, allowing single missiles to destroy hardened structures. During this operation, Iran deployed these precision guidance packages on warheads weighing more than one ton (1,000 kilograms), delivering high explosive yields directly onto high-value targets.

Upgraded Ballistic Systems: Khorramshahr-4 and Solid-Fuel Haj Qasem

The missile salvos utilized several of Iran's most advanced ballistic systems:

  • Khorramshahr-4 (خرمشهر 4): A heavy liquid-fueled missile with a range of 2,000 kilometers, carrying a guided warhead exceeding one ton.
  • Haj Qasem (حاج قاسم): Iran's first solid-fuel precision ballistic missile, featuring a range of 1,400 kilometers and an upgraded, highly destructive warhead.
  • Fattah and Kheibar: Hypersonic and precision-guided variants (including the Fattah system operated by Hezbollah) were deployed to penetrate Israel's terminal air defense networks.
  • Emad and Qadr: Upgraded 2026 variants equipped with maneuverable re-entry vehicles (MaRVs) featuring aerodynamic fins, enabling them to execute evasive maneuvers during the final phase of flight.

Countering the "No Military Power Remaining" Narrative

The scale of Operation True Promise 4 directly challenges the U.S. administration's public narrative. In a phone interview with CNBC news, Donald Trump claimed that the military campaign had effectively ended Iran's combat capabilities, stating that they had "no navy, no communications, no air force, and their missiles were scattered and destroyed."

By executing coordinated strikes across multiple countries on day 11 of the escalation, Iran demonstrated that its strategic command remains intact. The IRGC confirmed it retains full control over the Strait of Hormuz, challenging U.S. claims and warning that any attempt to escort oil tankers through the strait would be met with direct force.

Conclusion: The Horizon of Unrestricted Regional Warfare

The failure of the Trump-Putin diplomatic initiative and the launch of Operation True Promise 4 marks a significant escalation in the conflict. By deploying one-ton precision warheads against U.S. and Israeli installations, Iran has shown it can sustain high-intensity operations despite heavy bombardment.

As the U.S. and Israel continue their strategic bomber campaign, the lack of political constraints increases the risk of a wider regional conflict. The reliance on advanced ballistic guidance, heavy payloads, and coordinated coalition actions suggests that both sides are prepared for a long-term confrontation, changing the security dynamics of the Middle East.

item.title: True Promise 5: Joint Salvos Strike Israeli Bases
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: How Iran's True Promise 5 and Hezbollah's Al-Asf al-Ma'kool operations launched 150 missiles and drones, targeting Israeli command centers.
item.content:encoded:
True Promise 5: Joint Salvos Strike Israeli Bases

The military confrontation in the Middle East has expanded into a coordinated multi-front operation. Iran launched its "True Promise 5" (الوعد الصادق 5) campaign, targeting 54 strategic installations in Israel, while Hezbollah executed its own offensive code-named "Al-Asf al-Ma'kool" (العصف المأكول). The joint operation combined heavy ballistic missiles and drone swarms, striking targets from the northern border down to central Israel.

The Coordinated Front: True Promise 5 and Al-Asf al-Ma'kool

The alignment between Tehran and the Lebanese resistance has shifted from symbolic support to direct operational coordination. According to Israeli defense sources, the joint strike involved the launch of over 150 heavy missiles and 30 attack drones within a short window.

The IRGC confirmed the coordinated nature of the strikes, praising the effectiveness of the joint action. By launching simultaneous salvos from both western Iran and southern Lebanon, the joint front forced Israeli air defense systems to divide their tracking resources, allowing multiple projectiles to penetrate the airspace.

Heavy Salvos: Sating Northern and Central Israel

The strikes targeted key cities and settlements across northern and central Israel. In the north, heavy rocket salvos struck Metula and Kiryat Shmona—the latter targeted for the third time during this phase of the escalation.

Simultaneously, the HaSharon region in central Israel experienced major explosions as heavy missiles hit industrial and logistical sites. Further south, salvos targeted Katzrin in the southern Golan Heights, alongside drone strikes in Nahariya. The volume of incoming fire activated sirens across Tel Aviv and West Jerusalem, forcing millions of residents to seek shelter.

Targeting Command Centers: Dado and Stella Maris Bases

The joint operation focused on neutralizing command, control, and intelligence centers:

  • Stella Maris Base: Located in Haifa, this naval command facility was targeted by a swarm of suicide drones.
  • Dado Base: The headquarters of the IDF's Northern Command was struck by precision-guided missiles.
  • Ein Zitim Base: Located north of Safed, this intelligence facility was targeted by heavy salvos.
  • Ami'ad and Shimshon Bases: Staging grounds near the Sea of Galilee were targeted with upgraded rockets.
  • Misgav and Tira al-Karmel Bases: Logistical facilities in the Haifa sector suffered direct hits.

The Six-Week War Ceiling and Trump’s Ceasefire Shift

The timing of the joint offensive has coincided with political developments in Washington. Initially, U.S. President Donald Trump indicated that a regional ceasefire was "near" during a brief interview with a journalist from Axios and Channel 12. However, following the latest strikes, the White House shifted its wording, stating that a settlement was "not soon."

This political shift occurs as the U.S. and Israel work under a negotiated six-week ceiling for the war. Fearing that the U.S. administration might withdraw support due to threats to U.S. bases in the Gulf and oil price volatility, the Israeli military has intensified its campaign, seeking to degrade Iran's capabilities before the deadline expires.

Strategic Bomber Strikes on Qom: Shattering Rules of Engagement

The escalation reached a critical level following U.S. strategic bomber strikes targeting the Iranian city of Qom. U.S. heavy bombers hit civilian and industrial infrastructure in the area, signaling a shift in the campaign's parameters.

This strike has removed the remaining rules of engagement that had governed the conflict. By targeting historical and cultural centers like Qom, the coalition has expanded the scope of the war. In response, Iranian planners have standardized on heavy payloads, launching salvos against U.S. logistics nodes throughout the region.

The Paris Mechanism and the Threat of European Confrontation

On the diplomatic front, French, Syrian, and Lebanese representatives have attempted to implement the "Paris Mechanism." This framework seeks to preserve Syrian neutrality by securing the Lebanese-Syrian border, ignoring international disputes over the Golan Heights.

However, Paris has issued warnings to Tel Aviv regarding the targeting of Lebanese state infrastructure. France stated that any strikes disabling Lebanon's civilian power grid or transport networks would place Israel in direct political confrontation with Europe. This warning is supported by the presence of European UNIFIL forces and German naval assets operating in the eastern Mediterranean.

Conclusion: The Transition to an Unrestricted Regional War

The launch of Operation True Promise 5 and Hezbollah's Al-Asf al-Ma'kool marks a transition toward unrestricted regional warfare. By executing coordinated strikes against Israeli command centers and U.S. bases, the joint front has shown it can bypass regional air defense networks.

As the U.S. and Israel continue their bomber campaign and consider ground operations in southern Lebanon, the lack of political constraints increases the risk of a wider conflict. The presence of stealth UUV networks in the strait ensures that any attempt to bypass Iran's shipping regulations will carry a high risk of vessel loss, forcing a reassessment of naval operations in the region.

item.title: Quds Day Defiance: Leaders March, IDF HQ Targeted
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing the Quds Day rallies in Tehran, the drone strike targeting the IDF General Staff HQ in Tel Aviv, and the ground push toward the Litani.
item.content:encoded:
Quds Day Defiance: Leaders March, IDF HQ Targeted

Iran's annual Quds Day (يوم القدس) rallies have served as a platform for political and military defiance against the U.S.-led coalition. While U.S. and Israeli officials claimed the Iranian leadership had fled to underground bunkers following heavy bomber strikes, Tehran’s top officials walked openly in the streets among massive crowds. Simultaneously, a drone strike directly targeted the IDF General Staff Headquarters in Tel Aviv, highlighting the escalation of the conflict.

The Quds Day Rallies: Open Defiance in Tehran

The Quds Day rallies in Tehran saw millions of Iranians take to the streets, linking their national sovereignty directly to the Palestinian cause. The massive public participation was framed by local media as a demonstration of domestic support for the government during a period of high military tension.

The key detail of the rallies was the open participation of the state's top leadership. President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, defense policy chief Ali Larijani, and the head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) walked among the crowds, demonstrating that the government's control remains intact despite strategic bombardment.

Debunking the U.S. Bunkers Narrative

The open appearance of the Iranian leadership directly challenged U.S. and Israeli statements. In a joint press conference, the U.S. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth claimed that Iranian leaders were "hiding in deep underground bunkers," asserting that coalition air strikes had dismantled the regime's command structures.

By walking openly in the streets of Tehran without extensive defensive cordons, the leaders showed that these statements were inaccurate. Hebrew media outlets acknowledged the significance of this appearance, noting that it contradicted coalition assessments regarding the impact of the air campaign.

The Disconnect of the Exiled Opposition

The scale of the rallies also highlighted the political disconnect facing the exiled opposition. Reza Pahlavi, the son of the former Shah, issued public appeals urging the Iranian public to refrain from participating in the marches, claiming the government was on the verge of collapse.

However, the large crowds that responded to the state's call demonstrated that the exiled opposition's appeals had limited impact. This disconnect shows that domestic public opinion remains focused on national defense, prioritizing resistance against external military pressure over calls for internal change.

Hakirya Struck: Drone Strike on the IDF General Staff

While the rallies were underway in Tehran, a direct military message was delivered in Tel Aviv. A coordinated drone strike targeted the IDF General Staff Headquarters (Hakirya) in the heart of the city.

The strike occurred while public demonstrations were taking place in Tel Aviv, creating significant disruption. The drones bypassed local short-range defenses, impacting the command complex. This strike demonstrated that the command structure of the Israeli military remains vulnerable to precision strikes, even during periods of high alert.

Wave 45: Deploying the Kheibar Shekan Ballistic Missile

Following the Quds Day rallies, the IRGC launched Wave 45 of its counter-offensive. The strike relied on the Kheibar Shekan (خيبر شكن) ballistic missile, which has proven highly effective in penetrating air defense networks.

First deployed during the 12-day war in 2025 and utilized throughout the 2026 campaign, the Kheibar Shekan is recognized by Israeli analysts as a primary threat. Its high terminal velocity and maneuverability allow it to bypass the Arrow interceptor network, delivering high-explosive payloads onto strategic command hubs and airbase facilities.

Ground Push to the Litani: IDF 98th Division Mobilized

In Lebanon, the IDF has deployed a third division—the 98th Division—to push several kilometers deeper into Lebanese territory. The objective of the ground operation is to establish physical control over the area leading to the Litani River.

Israeli commanders have stated they do not trust the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) to enforce any disarmament agreements. By pushing toward the Litani, Israel aims to create a permanent buffer zone under its own authority, effectively bypassing the parameters of the November 2024 ceasefire agreement.

Conclusion: The Reshaping of the Levantine Map

The events of Quds Day demonstrate that the conflict is reshaping the geopolitical map of the Middle East. By ignoring UN resolutions and French mediation, the U.S. and Israel seek to establish a new security architecture in the Levant, marginalizing European influence in Lebanon and Syria.

However, the IDF's ground push has met stiff resistance, turning the border campaign into a war of attrition. As long as Iran sustains its missile salvos and its leadership maintains domestic support, the coalition's attempt to establish unilateral control over the region will face significant obstacles, extending the duration of the confrontation.

item.title: Strategic Expansion: Iran Targets Cyprus & Azerbaijan
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: How Iran and Hezbollah threaten to target Israeli military supply lines and staging bases in Cyprus, Crete, and Azerbaijan with heavy one-ton warheads.
item.content:encoded:
Strategic Expansion: Iran Targets Cyprus & Azerbaijan

The military confrontation in the Middle East is rapidly expanding beyond the immediate borders of Israel and Lebanon. In response to intensive U.S. and Israeli airstrikes, Iran and Hezbollah have warned they will target the external supply lines and staging bases that support Israeli air operations. The threat is concentrated on three vital regional chokepoints: Cyprus, Azerbaijan, and Syria.

Expanding the Target List: The Threat to Azerbaijan

Iran has expanded its strategic target list to include installations on Azerbaijani soil. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) recently demanded that Azerbaijan immediately expel the Israeli ambassador and shut down Israeli signals intelligence (SIGINT) facilities operating along the Iranian border.

Azerbaijan has long served as a critical forward base for Israeli intelligence and logistical operations. By targeting these installations, Tehran aims to neutralize surveillance hubs that monitor Iranian and Russian military activities, warning Baku that hosting foreign assets will carry a high cost.

The Cyprus Chokepoint: Countering British and Israeli Support Lines

Cyprus has emerged as a key logistics and support node for the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF). With domestic Israeli airfields frequently targeted by Hezbollah rocket salvos, Cyprus and Crete serve as vital staging areas for aircraft maintenance and supply flights.

Hezbollah has warned Cyprus that allowing its soil or British sovereign bases to be used for Israeli combat missions will result in direct retaliation. To reinforce this warning, Hezbollah demonstrated its readiness by preparing over 300 Fateh-110 precision ballistic missiles. In response, Turkey deployed F-16 fighters to northern Cyprus to monitor regional airspace, while the UK reinforced its military presence to secure its bases.

The Syrian Dilemma: Airspace Sensitivities and Interceptions

Syria remains a complex air defense node in the conflict. Israel and the United States utilize radar systems and air defense batteries stationed inside Syrian territory to monitor and intercept incoming missiles heading toward northern Israel.

For Iran, directly targeting these air defense assets inside Syria is complicated by regional geopolitical sensitivities. While Syrian forces remain integrated into the regional resistance framework, the presence of various international forces makes coordination challenging, creating a buffer zone that Israel exploits to intercept incoming threats before they reach its borders.

IRGC’s Heavy Warhead Strategy: Shifting to One-Ton Payloads

Brigadier General Majid Mousavi, Commander of the IRGC Aerospace Force, announced a major shift in Iran's ballistic missile doctrine. In future salvos, the minimum weight of Iranian missile warheads will be increased to no less than one ton (1,000 kilograms).

The introduction of these heavier warheads is designed to maximize the physical destruction of fortified installations, airfields, and underground command centers. The payloads will include specialized fragmentation and cluster warheads, designed to saturate large areas and disable runways with a single strike.

Bridging the Airpower Gap Against U.S. Bombers

The deployment of one-ton warheads is a direct response to the U.S. heavy bomber campaign. The United States has deployed B-1B Lancer, B-2 Spirit, and B-52 Stratofortress bombers from European and regional bases to conduct strikes inside Iran.

By increasing the weight and frequency of their missile salvos, Iranian commanders aim to offset the U.S. advantage in airpower. The strategy focuses on targeting the regional bases, radar hubs, and logistics lines that these bombers rely on, turning the conflict into a war of attrition against the coalition's infrastructure.

Grounding the IAF: Target-Isolation of External Airbases

The strategic objective of targeting Cyprus, Crete, and Azerbaijan is to isolate the Israeli Air Force (IAF). If domestic airfields in southern, central, and northern Israel are kept under constant fire, the IAF must rely on external facilities for staging and refueling.

By targeting the external infrastructure supporting these staging operations, the coalition aims to ground Israeli fighter jets. The loss of secure refueling and maintenance hubs in Cyprus or Azerbaijan would severely restrict the IAF's operational range, limiting its ability to sustain long-range operations.

Conclusion: A Multi-Front Regional Deterrence Balance

The potential expansion of the war to Cyprus and Azerbaijan represents a significant escalation. By targeting the logistical and intelligence nodes that support U.S. and Israeli air operations, Iran and Hezbollah are trying to establish a new regional balance of power.

This strategy is championed by U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose hawkish stance and crusader-themed tattoos reflect the ideological division of the conflict, as we documented and analyzed in our previous report. As the conflict intensifies, the willingness of regional states to host foreign military assets will be tested by the threat of heavy ballistic strikes, permanently altering the geopolitical landscape of the eastern Mediterranean.

item.title: Romania Defense Gaps: Trump Concessions to Russia
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing the hollowing out of Romania's air defenses (Aegis Ashore, Patriot) to reinforce the Gulf, and Trump's oil concessions to Putin.
item.content:encoded:
Romania Defense Gaps: Trump Concessions to Russia

The military confrontation in the Middle East has triggered a major realignment of global security assets, exposing vulnerabilities along NATO's eastern flank. To concentrate military resources against Iran, U.S. President Donald Trump has made significant geopolitical concessions to Russia, including lifting key restrictions on Russian oil exports. Simultaneously, the transfer of air defense missiles from European assets like Romania to the Persian Gulf has left key NATO installations exposed.

The Oil Concessions: Trump’s Lifeline to Putin

Under pressure from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Trump has altered U.S. policy toward Moscow. To prevent a catastrophic global fuel shortage, the U.S. administration lifted sanctions on Russian oil exports, delivering an estimated $150 million daily to the Russian treasury.

This policy shift represents a significant concession. European leaders have criticized the move, arguing that Trump is providing an economic lifeline to Moscow and prioritizing the conflict with Iran over the security of Ukraine and Eastern Europe. In response, Russian forces have paused active ground offensives in Ukraine, exploiting U.S. distraction to consolidate their gains.

Romania’s Strategic Access: The Mihail Kogălniceanu Agreement

As part of the U.S. campaign against Iran, Romania has approved a request to host U.S. forces and specialized assets. The agreement grants the U.S. military permission to use Mihail Kogălniceanu Airbase to support operations in the Middle East.

While Romanian officials emphasize that the hosted assets are defensive in nature, the decision has raised security concerns in Bucharest. By acting as a transit hub for U.S. operations, Romania risks exposing its own territory to retaliatory long-range strikes from regional forces.

Hollowing Out Romania’s Patriot Batteries

The primary security risk facing Romania is the depletion of its domestic air defense network. Bucharest initially operated four Patriot batteries, but transferred one to Ukraine to support defense operations, leaving three units.

Of the remaining three, only one battery is fully operational due to maintenance and training delays. To cover the gaps, Greece deployed a single Patriot battery near the Bulgaria-Romania border. However, the overall coverage remains fragmented, and the system is vulnerable to high-volume attacks.

The 85-Missile Math: Exposing NATO’s Eastern Flank

The vulnerability of Romania's defensive network is worsened by the transfer of interceptor stockpiles to the Middle East. U.S. planners have stripped Romania's inventory of PAC-3 MSE missiles to replenish bases in the Gulf and reinforce Israel.

Open-source intelligence estimates suggest Romania's total interceptor inventory has fallen to approximately 170 missiles. Assuming a standard engagement protocol of firing two interceptors per target at a 100% success rate, it would only take a salvo of 85 ballistic missiles to completely exhaust Romania's air defenses, leaving NATO's eastern flank exposed.

Aegis Ashore: Ground-Based Interceptors Under Strain

In addition to Patriot batteries, Romania hosts the Aegis Ashore ballistic missile defense site. The facility utilizes SM-3 interceptors launched from MK-41 Vertical Launch System (VLS) cells, supported by the SPY-1 radar system.

While Aegis Ashore was designed to defend Europe against long-range ballistic threats, U.S. planners have redirected satellite communication assets and tracking resources from the Romanian site to support operations in the Gulf. This redirection of sensor capacity has degraded the Aegis Ashore's early warning capabilities, leaving the facility vulnerable to high-velocity maneuvers.

Opportunistic Alignment: Moscow and Beijing’s Silence

The reallocation of NATO assets has occurred alongside a calculated silence from Moscow and Beijing. Rather than intervening to support Iran, Russia and China are utilizing the crisis to negotiate economic and strategic advantages from Washington.

Iran previously provided Russia with crucial Shahed drones and tactical advice during the early phases of the Ukraine war. Now, Moscow is exploiting U.S. vulnerability to secure sanction relief, choosing silent complicity in the campaign against Iran in exchange for immediate economic gains. This opportunism shows that both powers prioritize their immediate interests over ideological alliances.

Conclusion: The Reshaping of Global Alliance Architecture

The hollowing out of Romania's air defenses and the lifting of Russian oil sanctions demonstrate the changing parameters of global security. By shifting Patriot missiles and communication resources from Europe to the Gulf, the U.S. has compromised the defense of NATO's eastern flank.

As Russia secures oil revenues and Romania's airspace remains vulnerable to saturation, the costs of the U.S. campaign against Iran are being borne by European allies. The collapse of the post-Cold War containment strategy suggests that the Middle East conflict is accelerating the fragmentation of NATO, creating opportunities for Moscow and Beijing to consolidate their spheres of influence.

item.title: Radar Blown: Drone Destroys Saudi AN/FPS-117 Near Qaisumah
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing the IRGC drone strike destroying a Saudi AN/FPS-117 AESA radar in Qaisumah, exposing gaps in the Peace Shield defense network.
item.content:encoded:
Radar Blown: Drone Destroys Saudi AN/FPS-117 Near Qaisumah

A targeted IRGC suicide drone strike has destroyed a strategic Saudi AN/FPS-117 early warning radar near Qaisumah in northeastern Saudi Arabia. The strike, occurring on March 7, 2026, has bypassed the Kingdom's multi-layered air defense grid and created a significant blind spot in its northeastern early warning corridor. The targeting of Saudi assets highlights the vulnerability of regional military infrastructure that supports U.S. air operations following the withdrawal of the aircraft carrier USS Gerald R. Ford.

The Strike: Blinding the Peace Shield Network near Qaisumah

The strike took place in the early hours near the border town of Qaisumah, close to the military staging zone of Hafar al-Batin. A single Iranian-manufactured suicide drone, operating at low altitude, bypassed local radar detection systems.

The drone directly targeted the rotating array of the active AN/FPS-117 radar station. The impact and subsequent explosion destroyed the transmitter-receiver modules, disabling the station. The loss of this node blinds the early warning coverage that monitors the airspace bordering Iraq and Iran.

Technical Profile of the AN/FPS-117 AESA Radar

The AN/FPS-117, produced by Lockheed Martin, is a 3D long-range, L-band Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) radar. Key technical features include:

  • Operational Range: Provides continuous 3D tracking of aircraft, drones, and ballistic missiles at distances up to 470 kilometers.
  • Electronic Countermeasures: Utilizes 18-channel frequency hopping to maintain search capabilities under intense electronic jamming.
  • Global Standard: The system is the standard long-range surveillance radar used by the U.S. and Canada for northern warning systems, and is operated by Germany (RRP-117) and the UK (Type 92).

Grounding U.S. Aviation: The Link to Prince Sultan Airbase

The targeting of the Qaisumah radar is linked to U.S. operations. With the aircraft carrier USS Gerald R. Ford withdrawn to Souda Bay due to structural damage from a 30-hour fire, the Pentagon relocated its carrier-based F-35C and F-15E strike fighters to Prince Sultan Airbase (PSAB) in central Saudi Arabia.

To support these jets and coordinate refueling tanker paths, Saudi Arabia activated its "Peace Shield" (درع السلام) radar network, sharing real-time tracking data with U.S. forces. By disabling the early warning sensors that protect the northern corridor, the IRGC has made U.S. operations out of PSAB more vulnerable.

Complicity Disclosed: Trump’s Claims of Gulf Cooperation

While Saudi officials have maintained a public stance of neutrality, declaring that their airspace is not used for offensive operations, Donald Trump challenged this narrative. During his public addresses, Trump stated that Gulf nations are actively facilitating U.S. strikes.

This public disclosure turned Saudi air defense installations into military targets. The IRGC has argued that by utilizing the Peace Shield network to coordinate and protect U.S. jets striking Iranian territory, Saudi Arabia has integrated its defense infrastructure into the coalition's campaign, justifying retaliatory strikes.

Depleting the Peace Shield: Impact on Northeastern Airspace

Before the current conflict, the Royal Saudi Air Force operated a fleet of 17 AN/FPS-117 units as the backbone of its Peace Shield air defense network. The latest strike, following a similar attack on a eastern-sector radar, means at least two units have been destroyed, leaving 15 operational.

Because these radars are static, replacing them requires years of logistics and procurement. The destruction of the Qaisumah station leaves the northeastern border—historically a sensitive sector since the Gulf War—exposed to low-altitude drone and cruise missile penetration.

The Regional Pattern: Systematically Targeting Air Defense Hubs

The strike on the Saudi radar is part of a regional pattern targeting coalition air defense systems. To prepare corridors for ballistic missile salvos, regional forces have systematically targeted early warning and interceptor batteries:

  • Jordan: A U.S.-operated THAAD launcher was targeted and disabled.
  • United Arab Emirates: Two THAAD launcher complexes were hit by precision drones.
  • Saudi Arabia: The destruction of the AN/FPS-117 near Qaisumah blinds the radar envelope that feeds into Saudi Patriot batteries.

Conclusion: The Vulnerability of Joint Defense Operations

The drone strike destroying the AN/FPS-117 radar near Qaisumah highlights the difficulty of protecting static early warning installations from low-altitude threats. By targeting the nodes that sustain U.S. flight corridors, the IRGC has shown that Gulf air defense networks can be penetrated.

As Saudi Arabia manages the gaps in its northeastern radar coverage and U.S. forces adjust their flight paths, the limits of the Peace Shield are clear. The vulnerability of these early warning stations suggests that regional cooperation with U.S. military operations carries high security risks, exposing domestic infrastructure to retaliatory strikes.

item.title: Sejgil-2 Debut: Eilat Struck, US Consulate Hit
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing the combat debut of Iran's Sejgil-2 solid-fuel missile in Eilat and the strike damaging the U.S. Consulate in Tel Aviv.
item.content:encoded:
Sejgil-2 Debut: Eilat Struck, US Consulate Hit

The current conflict has seen the operational debut of Iran's Sejgil (سجيل) series, a two-stage, solid-fuel medium-range ballistic missile (MRBM). While used in previous rounds, the Sejgil has made its first appearance in the current campaign, with launches targeting Eilat's "Black Industrial Zone." Concurrently, consecutive missile waves directed at Tel Aviv have resulted in heavy structural damage to the U.S. Consulate building, highlighting the intensity of the latest salvos.

The Combat Debut: Sejgil Ballistic Missiles Enter the Conflict

Iranian state television officially announced that the IRGC has integrated the Sejgil ballistic missile series into its active operations. Although Sejgil units were deployed during Operation True Promise 3 on June 18, 2025, they had not been utilized in the current round of fighting until now.

The deployment of the Sejgil series represents a significant escalation in the warhead payload and terminal velocity directed at coalition coordinates. The missile's high-speed reentry profile has prompted Israeli military investigators to audit the guidance systems utilized during the latest strike.

Eilat’s Black Industrial Zone Targeted

The target of the first Sejgil strike was the "Black Industrial Zone" in the southern port city of Eilat. The zone contains critical logistics, storage, and industrial infrastructure that supports both civilian trade and military staging.

Despite local air defense coverage, the warhead penetrated the airspace and impacted the industrial sector. The strike caused extensive fires and structural damage, demonstrating the capability of long-range ballistic missiles to hit specific industrial assets at distances exceeding 2,000 kilometers from launch points in central Iran.

The Technical Audit: Sejgil-1 vs. Sejgil-2 Guidance

Israeli military and intelligence services are conducting an audit to determine whether the missile was a Sejgil-1 or the newer Sejgil-2 variant:

  • Sejgil-1: The baseline variant has a Circular Error Probable (CEP) of approximately 50 meters, with its warhead remaining unguided during the terminal phase of flight.
  • Sejgil-2: The upgraded variant features aerodynamic control surfaces (fins) on the warhead, reducing the CEP to under 10 meters. It utilizes a combined guidance system of Inertial Navigation (INS) and GPS, operating solely on INS during the final phase to bypass GPS jamming.

Penetrating Air Defenses: Evasion of Arrow-3 Networks

The Sejgil's terminal reentry velocity of Mach 11 to Mach 13–14 presents a severe challenge for terminal air defense systems. The high velocity reduces detection times and leaves little margin for interceptor calculations.

While Israeli defense officials claimed that the Arrow-3 (Hetz-3) system intercepted the threat, local reports and damage tracking confirmed the warhead impacted its target. The penetration of the defensive envelope shows that current interceptor models cannot consistently neutralize high-velocity, maneuvering solid-fuel targets. Only the under-development Arrow-4 system is designed to engage threats in this speed class.

Solid-Fuel Propulsion: Strategic Speed and Mobility

The defining feature of the Sejgil is its two-stage, solid-fuel composite rocket motor. Solid-fuel propulsion offers significant advantages over older liquid-fueled missiles like the Shahab series:

  • Launch Readiness: Solid-fuel missiles do not require fueling before launch and can be prepared and fired from mobile launchers within minutes.
  • Mobility: The stable solid fuel allows launchers to transit rough terrain without risk of fuel leaks, making the batteries difficult to locate and destroy before launch.
  • Safety: The composite fuel is safer to store and handle, reducing the logistical footprint of launch units.

Strike on the U.S. Consulate in Tel Aviv

The deployment of the Sejgil occurred alongside a continuous 90-minute wave of attacks targeting central Israel since midnight. Heavy missile strikes directed at Tel Aviv resulted in a direct hit near the U.S. Consulate building.

A large shrapnel fragment from a heavy ballistic missile impacted the facility, causing significant structural damage to the consulate's exterior and offices. While Israel claimed to have intercepted the incoming missile, the size of the fragment indicates a heavy warhead was involved, and the strike coincided with cluster rocket salvos launched by Hezbollah against northern coordinates.

Conclusion: The Expanding Range of Iranian Missiles

The combat debut of the Sejgil-2 in the current war highlights the limitations of the coalition's defensive network. By demonstrating the ability to prepare, launch, and guide a Mach 13 solid-fuel missile from central Iran to Eilat in under seven minutes, the IRGC has established a persistent strategic threat.

As the U.S. and Israel assess the damage to Eilat and the Tel Aviv consulate, the strategic calculations for the conflict are changing. The availability of high-velocity, solid-fuel systems suggests that future targets will remain vulnerable to precision strikes, regardless of the density of the air defense networks deployed to protect them.
