item.title: Point Blind: Drone Destroys US Embassy C-RAM in Iraq
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing the single drone strike that bypassed and destroyed the U.S. Embassy's C-RAM air defense system in Baghdad's Green Zone.
item.content:encoded:
Point Blind: Drone Destroys US Embassy C-RAM in Iraq

A single precision-guided suicide drone has penetrated the airspace of Baghdad's Green Zone, bypassing and destroying the U.S. Embassy's primary air defense system. The incident has raised serious questions within the Pentagon regarding the effectiveness of point defense systems against low-flying, autonomous threats. The destruction of the C-RAM (Counter-Rocket, Artillery, and Mortar) unit occurred alongside damage to the embassy's secure satellite communications and heliport, disrupting operations in Iraq.

The Incident: Single Drone Strike Strikedown in the Green Zone

The strike occurred in the early morning of Saturday, March 14, 2026. A single suicide drone, operating at low altitude to minimize radar detection, entered the airspace of the diplomatic compound in Baghdad.

The drone directly targeted the embassy's active point defense system. Unlike saturation attacks that rely on overwhelming numbers to exhaust interceptors, this operation succeeded with a single asset, indicating a high degree of target guidance. The strike has prompted the State Department to evaluate the feasibility of sustaining diplomatic operations in Iraq under the current security conditions.

The Vulnerability of the C-RAM Point Defense System

The C-RAM system is designed to provide point defense for high-value installations, utilizing a high-rate-of-fire rotary cannon to shred incoming mortar shells, rockets, and drones at close range. It represents the absolute final line of defense.

The fact that a single drone bypassed the C-RAM's tracking loop and struck the system itself has shocked defense analysts. The failure indicates that the system's sensors were either blinded or failed to resolve the drone's low-radar-cross-section profile in time, allowing the weapon to impact the radar and firing unit directly.

Satellite Communications and Embassy Heliport Damaged

The destruction of the C-RAM was accompanied by secondary damage to the embassy's operational infrastructure. The blast and resulting fire damaged the secure satellite communications dish, which is used to transmit classified diplomatic data.

Furthermore, shrapnel from the impact damaged the heliport located within the embassy compound, compromising the facility's emergency evacuation corridor. While no U.S. personnel casualties were reported in the blast, the destruction of the point defense system has left the remaining embassy personnel exposed to further attacks.

The Karrada Strike Context and Timeline

The drone strike took place approximately one hour after a U.S. air strike on the Karrada neighborhood of Baghdad. The U.S. raid had targeted a regional cell, killing three pro-Iranian fighters.

The rapid execution of the counter-strike on the embassy suggests that the drone unit was in a state of high readiness, awaiting targeting coordinates. The close synchronization of the events shows that the resistance forces in Iraq possess the capability to execute immediate, targeted responses to U.S. military actions within the capital.

AI and Optical Navigation: Iran’s Technology Transfer

The precision of the drone strike indicates the use of advanced guidance systems. Analysts suggest the drone utilized artificial intelligence-based target recognition and optical navigation, bypassing the electronic warfare systems deployed around the Green Zone.

By relying on visual tracking algorithms rather than GPS signals, the drone remained immune to GPS jamming. The success of the strike confirms that Iran has transferred these optical guidance technologies to its regional partners, allowing them to locate and target specific components of air defense systems on the ground.

Strategic Implications for Israeli Air Defense Models

The destruction of the C-RAM in Baghdad has strategic implications for Israel's defense planning. Point defense systems like the Iron Dome and David's Sling rely on similar radar and tracking principles to coordinate interceptors.

If low-cost, AI-guided drones can systematically target and destroy these tracking sensors, Israel's defensive shield could be disabled. In response to this threat, Israeli defense analysts have urged the IDF to abandon defensive doctrines, focusing instead on preemptive strikes to target drone warehouses on the ground before the weapons can be launched.

Conclusion: The Threat to Point Defense Infrastructures

The single drone strike on the U.S. Embassy's C-RAM highlights the vulnerability of static point defenses to autonomous weapons. The ability to neutralize a multi-million-dollar defense system with a single low-cost drone changes the tactical balance for military bases.

As the U.S. military evaluates the damage to its communication networks and plans potential evacuations from Iraq, the limits of current defensive tech are clear. The proliferation of optical-navigation drones suggests that securing military and diplomatic installations will require physical barriers and preemptive options, as electronic defense systems are no longer sufficient to guarantee safety.

Unlike saturation attacks that rely on overwhelming numbers to exhaust interceptors, this operation succeeded with a single asset, indicating a high degree of target guidance. The strike has prompted the State Department to evaluate the feasibility of sustaining diplomatic operations in Iraq under the current security conditions.

The Vulnerability of the C-RAM Point Defense System

The C-RAM system is designed to provide point defense for high-value installations, utilizing a high-rate-of-fire rotary cannon to shred incoming mortar shells, rockets, and drones at close range. It represents the absolute final line of defense.

The fact that a single drone bypassed the C-RAM's tracking loop and struck the system itself has shocked defense analysts. The failure indicates that the system's sensors were either blinded or failed to resolve the drone's low-radar-cross-section profile in time, allowing the weapon to impact the radar and firing unit directly.

Satellite Communications and Embassy Heliport Damaged

The destruction of the C-RAM was accompanied by secondary damage to the embassy's operational infrastructure. The blast and resulting fire damaged the secure satellite communications dish, which is used to transmit classified diplomatic data.

Furthermore, shrapnel from the impact damaged the heliport located within the embassy compound, compromising the facility's emergency evacuation corridor. While no U.S. personnel casualties were reported in the blast, the destruction of the point defense system has left the remaining embassy personnel exposed to further attacks.

The Karrada Strike Context and Timeline

The drone strike took place approximately one hour after a U.S. air strike on the Karrada neighborhood of Baghdad. The U.S. raid had targeted a regional cell, killing three pro-Iranian fighters.

The rapid execution of the counter-strike on the embassy suggests that the drone unit was in a state of high readiness, awaiting targeting coordinates. The close synchronization of the events shows that the resistance forces in Iraq possess the capability to execute immediate, targeted responses to U.S. military actions within the capital.

AI and Optical Navigation: Iran’s Technology Transfer

The precision of the drone strike indicates the use of advanced guidance systems. Analysts suggest the drone utilized artificial intelligence-based target recognition and optical navigation, bypassing the electronic warfare systems deployed around the Green Zone.

By relying on visual tracking algorithms rather than GPS signals, the drone remained immune to GPS jamming. The success of the strike confirms that Iran has transferred these optical guidance technologies to its regional partners, allowing them to locate and target specific components of air defense systems on the ground.

Strategic Implications for Israeli Air Defense Models

The destruction of the C-RAM in Baghdad has strategic implications for Israel's defense planning. Point defense systems like the Iron Dome and David's Sling rely on similar radar and tracking principles to coordinate interceptors.

If low-cost, AI-guided drones can systematically target and destroy these tracking sensors, Israel's defensive shield could be disabled. In response to this threat, Israeli defense analysts have urged the IDF to abandon defensive doctrines, focusing instead on preemptive strikes to target drone warehouses on the ground before the weapons can be launched.

Conclusion: The Threat to Point Defense Infrastructures

The single drone strike on the U.S. Embassy's C-RAM highlights the vulnerability of static point defenses to autonomous weapons. The ability to neutralize a multi-million-dollar defense system with a single low-cost drone changes the tactical balance for military bases.

As the U.S. military evaluates the damage to its communication networks and plans potential evacuations from Iraq, the limits of current defensive tech are clear. The proliferation of optical-navigation drones suggests that securing military and diplomatic installations will require physical barriers and preemptive options, as electronic defense systems are no longer sufficient to guarantee safety.

item.title: Somaliland Proposes US Military Move to Berbera
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing Somaliland's proposal to transfer Al Udeid and the US Fifth Fleet to Berbera, Israel's role, and Horn of Africa geopolitics.
item.content:encoded:
Somaliland Proposes US Military Move to Berbera

The breakaway East African republic of Somaliland has issued a public proposal to the United States, offering to host U.S. air and naval assets currently stationed in the Persian Gulf. Brokered by Israel, the proposal suggests transferring major assets, including the Al Udeid Air Base and the U.S. Navy Fifth Fleet, to the port city of Berbera. The development highlights a shifting geopolitical alignment that seeks to bypass host nation constraints in the Gulf and counter Chinese influence in the Horn of Africa.

The Proposal: Somaliland Offers Berbera to the U.S.

The Republic of Somaliland, which declared independence from Somalia in 1991 but remains unrecognized by most of the international community, has officially invited Washington to establish a military presence in its territory.

The proposal offers the port of Berbera as a new home for U.S. regional forces. Specifically, Somaliland suggests relocating the Al Udeid Air Base, currently in Qatar, and the U.S. Navy Fifth Fleet, currently in Bahrain. In exchange, Somaliland seeks official U.S. and international diplomatic recognition, alongside a formal strategic security partnership.

Access to Critical Minerals and Off-Shore Energy Blocks

To sweeten the deal, Somaliland has offered the U.S. exclusive economic concessions. According to documents attached to the official proposal, Washington would receive exclusive mining rights to Somaliland's untapped natural resources, including lithium, gold, copper, tin, and gypsum.

Further, the proposal grants exclusive exploration and drilling rights in 24 offshore and onshore blocks. These blocks hold estimated oil and gas reserves of between 1 and 5 billion barrels. Somaliland has indicated that these assets are ready for development in partnership with Western energy companies, including Genel Energy and RAK Gas.

Israel’s Diplomatic Mediation and Geopolitical Ambitions

The diplomatic initiative is heavily backed by Israel, which remains the only state to have formally recognized Somaliland's independence. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has encouraged the U.S. administration to accept the offer, seeking to establish a non-Arab ally near the Red Sea.

Israeli planners view the relocation of U.S. bases as a method to achieve two goals: removing U.S. forces from vulnerable positions in the Gulf, and drawing the U.S. into a direct confrontation with Iran. By promoting Somaliland as a secure alternative, Israel aims to facilitate a broader strategic realignment in the region.

The Relocation Calculus: Dismantling Gulf Base Dependency

The proposal aligns with discussions in Washington regarding the future of U.S. bases in the GCC. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and National Security Advisor Michael Waltz have reportedly noted that U.S. forces in the Gulf face high vulnerabilities due to local political pressure and proximity to Iranian strike networks.

Since the U.S. does not pay direct lease fees for several of its Gulf installations, planners are less constrained by real estate investments. Relocating to Berbera would allow the U.S. military to operate with greater independence, free from the host nation restrictions that limit operations launched from Qatar or Bahrain.

The Horn of Africa: Confronting China’s Presence in Djibouti

A primary strategic advantage of the Berbera proposal is its proximity to neighboring Djibouti. Djibouti hosts China's first overseas military base, establishing a key node for Beijing's maritime security network in the Indian Ocean.

By establishing a major air and naval hub in Berbera, the U.S. military would place itself directly adjacent to the Chinese facility. This footprint would allow the U.S. to integrate operations across Central Command (CENTCOM) and Africa Command (AFRICOM), using partners like Egypt to counter Chinese economic and military influence in East Africa.

Regional Backlash: The Fallout in Saudi Arabia and the UAE

The proposed Israel-Somaliland axis has caused significant concern in Riyadh and Abu Dhabi. Saudi Arabia views the presence of an Israeli-backed state on the Horn of Africa as a threat to its southern security, prompting it to alter its strategy in Yemen.

Riyadh actively worked to disrupt the UAE-brokered federal projects in Yemen, which sought to establish control over Bab el-Mandeb. The collapse of these projects, combined with the strategic retreat of the UAE model (which sought to act as the "Switzerland of the Arabs" while intervening in regional conflicts), has left local states exposed to retaliatory pressure from both Iran and Western lobbies.

Conclusion: A New Security Architecture Beyond the Arab World

The Somaliland proposal highlights the changing priorities of U.S. and Israeli strategic planning. By offering Berbera as an alternative to Gulf bases, Somaliland has provided the U.S. with a method to bypass local political constraints while maintaining surveillance over Bab el-Mandeb and the Red Sea.

As the U.S. administration evaluates the economic and mineral concessions, the future of the Gulf bases remains uncertain. If the relocation proceeds, it will mark the end of the post-Gulf War security architecture, shifting the focus of U.S. power projection to the Horn of Africa and creating a direct line of confrontation with both regional forces and Chinese global influence.

item.title: South Pars Struck: US Strips European Air Defenses
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing the U.S.-Israeli strike on Iran's South Pars gas field in Asaluyeh, Trump's reallocation of European Patriots, and Gulf shifts.
item.content:encoded:
South Pars Struck: US Strips European Air Defenses

U.S. and Israeli air strikes have targeted Iran's South Pars gas field in Asaluyeh, halting production in two refineries and disrupting regional energy infrastructure. The escalation comes as U.S. President Donald Trump orders the removal of NATO's air defense systems and ammunition stockpiles from Europe to the Middle East, penalizing European nations for remaining neutral in the conflict. Fearing the vulnerability of their own energy networks, Gulf capitals are accelerating diplomatic options, pivoting toward Chinese models for long-term security.

South Pars Struck: Disruption in Asaluyeh Refineries

The air strikes directly targeted Phases 5, 10, and 14 of the South Pars gas field in Asaluyeh. According to energy analyst Olga Sidorova, the strikes halted production at two major refineries, cutting off 100 million cubic meters of daily gas output.

Iranian military officials labeled the attack a "war crime" targeting the economic infrastructure of the Iranian population, pledging that the action would face retaliatory operations. The strikes aim to degrade Iran's domestic energy capacity, but the fallout is expected to affect regional gas distribution networks.

Gulf Complicity: Basing Sorties and the Qatari Dilemma

The strikes on Asaluyeh were executed by U.S. and Israeli aircraft operating out of bases in the Persian Gulf, including Prince Sultan Airbase in Saudi Arabia. This involvement has created a diplomatic dilemma for regional states like Qatar.

The South Pars field is shared between Iran and Qatar, where it is known as the North Dome. Qatari authorities issued diplomatic statements that avoided direct criticism of the U.S. while expressing concern over the targeting of shared assets. Qatar remains dependent on the U.S. defense umbrella, leaving the country unable to block U.S. forces from utilizing local infrastructure for strike missions.

The Retaliation Risk: Threats to Chevron and Gulf Joint Fields

Tehran has warned that because Gulf nations are hosting U.S. strike aircraft, they will bear the security consequences. The IRGC announced that any strikes on Iranian infrastructure will lead to direct retaliatory operations against U.S. corporate assets in the Gulf.

The primary targets for these counter-strikes include joint offshore fields and U.S. corporate operations, such as Chevron facilities in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar. This threat has alarmed Western energy companies, which do not want to see their multi-billion-dollar investments destroyed in a conflict over regional hegemony.

Trump’s European Retaliation: Stripping NATO Air Defenses

Trump's campaign in the Middle East has also impacted European security. Highly frustrated by the refusal of European NATO allies to deploy minesweepers and warships to help break the Hormuz blockade, Trump ordered the reallocation of NATO defense assets.

The commander of the U.S. European Command confirmed that Patriot batteries, THAAD systems, and advanced interceptor stockpiles have been removed from Europe and shipped to the Middle East. This reallocation aims to protect U.S. bases in the Gulf and support Israeli defense networks, leaving Europe's eastern flank exposed.

European Security Fallout: Delays in Patriot and Ammunition Delivery

The relocation of air defense assets has caused delays in the delivery of military equipment to European capitals:

  • Ammunition Depletion: Stockpiles of Patriot missiles and artillery munitions designated for Eastern Europe have been redirected to the Gulf.
  • Contract Delays: Delivery schedules for European defense contracts have been suspended to prioritize Middle East operations.

European leaders have criticized this policy shift, arguing that Trump is compromising European defense stability to sustain his campaign against Iran.

Shifting Autonomy: French and German Strategic Defense Pivots

In response to U.S. volatility, France and Germany are accelerating their strategic autonomy initiatives:

  • FCAS Project: Joint development of the Future Combat Air System (FCAS) has received increased funding to reduce reliance on U.S. military hardware.
  • Independent Deployments: France deployed its own aircraft carrier to the region to protect French maritime interests in the Gulf, maintaining a policy independent of U.S. command.

While Germany expressed understanding of the security goals against Iran, both nations are adjusting to a security landscape where U.S. commitments are no longer reliable.

Conclusion: The Gulf’s Pivot Toward Chinese Development Models

The strikes on South Pars and the hollowing out of European air defenses show the strategic costs of the U.S. campaign in the Gulf. Despite spending trillions on Western defense contracts over the decades, Gulf nations realize that their energy infrastructure remains vulnerable to both Iranian strikes and U.S. escalation.

Fearing that Trump is willing to compromise regional stability to secure his political legacy, Gulf capitals are looking to China. They conclude that long-term stability must be built on economic development and diplomatic mediation—represented by the Chinese model—rather than the military alliances of the West, which treat the region as a funding vehicle for proxy wars.

item.title: Submarine Fires from Turkish Waters to Hit Natanz
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: A submarine launched missiles from waters between Turkey and Northern Cyprus targeting Iran's Natanz, triggering a sovereignty crisis with Ankara and exposing NATO fault lines.
item.content:encoded:
Submarine Fires from Turkish Waters to Hit Natanz

A submarine launched multiple cruise missiles from waters between Turkey and Northern Cyprus, targeting Iran's Natanz nuclear enrichment facility over a trajectory crossing Syria and Iraq. Fishermen off the Karpasia peninsula village of Bafra captured video of the launch, triggering panic across Turkish-controlled Northern Cyprus and a sovereignty crisis between Ankara and the U.S.-Israeli coalition. Turkey scrambled F-16s and initiated a submarine hunt, but the vessel had already departed. The incident represents a deliberate provocation against Erdogan, using Turkish territorial waters as a launchpad for strikes on Iran without Ankara's knowledge or consent.

The Launch: Missiles from the Karpasia Coast

Multiple missiles were launched from waters off the village of Bafra on the Karpasia peninsula, the northeastern finger of Northern Cyprus that faces directly toward Turkey across a narrow strait. The launch was captured on video by local fishermen from multiple angles, providing irrefutable visual evidence.

The smoke trail rose at a low angle before climbing eastward, consistent with a cruise missile trajectory over Syria and Iraq toward Iran. The timing of the launch coincided precisely with the strikes on Natanz reported earlier in the day, confirming that the submarine served as one of the launch platforms for the attack on Iran's primary uranium enrichment facility.

Virginia Class or Dolphin-2: The Identity Question

Turkish and regional intelligence agencies are working to determine whether the submarine was American or Israeli:

The Virginia-Class Hypothesis (U.S.)

  • A Virginia-class nuclear-powered attack submarine (SSN) from the USS Gerald R. Ford carrier strike group is known to be operating in the Eastern Mediterranean.
  • The submarine did not transit the Suez Canal with the carrier group and remained in the Eastern Mediterranean.
  • The Karpasia peninsula's underwater geography has been identified by U.S. naval planners as suitable for submarine operations targeting Iran from the Mediterranean vector.
  • The stealth capabilities of a nuclear submarine would explain why Turkish radars and coast guard patrols failed to detect the vessel.

The Dolphin-2 Hypothesis (Israel)

  • Israel's Dolphin-2 class submarines are diesel-electric vessels built in Germany, equipped with torpedo tubes capable of launching cruise missiles.
  • According to U.S. documents, all Israeli Dolphin-class submarines are currently deployed outside Israeli territorial waters.
  • 99% of Israeli submarines are operating beyond their home waters, dispersed across the Mediterranean and potentially the Indian Ocean.
  • The Dolphin-2 could have launched Popeye Turbo SLCM cruise missiles with sufficient range to reach Natanz via a Syria-Iraq flight path.

The prevailing assessment is that both platforms may have been involved: a Virginia-class providing the primary strike capability while a Dolphin-2 operated in coordination.

The Provocation: Erdogan's Warning and Netanyahu's Answer

The submarine launch was a direct response to President Erdogan's recent statement at a public gathering:

"The Middle East is boiling now. Zionist Israel has committed massacres against hundreds of thousands of people, and I have no doubt it will pay the price for this."

Netanyahu's answer came not in words but in action: launching missiles from waters adjacent to Turkish sovereign territory, demonstrating that Israel can project force through Turkey's sphere of influence without detection or permission.

The message to Erdogan is threefold:

  1. Your territorial waters are permeable: Turkish naval surveillance failed to detect the submarine before, during, or after the launch.
  2. Your F-16s arrived too late: By the time Turkey scrambled fighters, the submarine and its missiles were gone.
  3. Your threats have no operational backing: If Turkey cannot detect a submarine in its own coastal waters, its military threats against Israel lack credibility.

Turkey's Detection Failure: The Stealth Gap

The incident exposed a critical vulnerability in Turkey's naval surveillance architecture:

  • Radar failure: Neither coastal radars nor naval surveillance systems detected the submarine's approach, presence, or departure.
  • Coast guard blind: Turkish coast guard patrols in the area between Turkey and Northern Cyprus did not identify the submarine or its launch preparations.
  • Sonar gap: Turkey's anti-submarine warfare capabilities in the Eastern Mediterranean proved insufficient to detect a modern submarine operating in stealth mode.
  • Discovery by fishermen: The launch was first detected not by the Turkish military but by civilian fishermen who filmed the missile exhaust plume, a humiliating revelation for NATO's second-largest military.

Turkey has deployed F-16 fighters to Northern Cyprus and initiated a search for the submarine, but military analysts assess that the vessel has already withdrawn to deeper Mediterranean waters beyond Turkish detection range.

The Sovereignty Violation: International Law

The legal dimensions of the incident are severe regardless of whether the submarine operated in territorial or international waters:

If launched from Turkish/Northern Cyprus territorial waters:

  • This constitutes a direct violation of Turkish sovereignty under international law.
  • The use of another state's territorial waters to launch an attack on a third country is an act of belligerence that implicates the territorial state.
  • Turkey would have legal grounds to treat this as an act of war.

If launched from international waters between Turkey and Northern Cyprus:

  • Even from international waters, launching cruise missiles in close proximity to Turkish military bases (including the Turkish naval facility at Famagusta) represents a hostile act.
  • The flight path of the missiles over or near Turkish-controlled airspace adds an additional sovereignty concern.
  • The U.S. and Israel effectively treated the waters around Cyprus as if they were under their own sovereignty, as Turkish media noted.

Northern Cyprus's Presidential Media Center initially issued a statement claiming that reports of missiles launched from within its territorial waters "do not correspond to reality," a denial that Ankara pressured Nicosia to make despite the video evidence filmed from multiple angles by fishermen.

The Greek Cyprus Angle: Base Access Questions

The involvement of Greek Cypriot territory adds another layer of complexity:

  • Greek Cyprus hosts British Sovereign Base Areas (Akrotiri and Dhekelia) that have been used for Western military operations in the region.
  • It is possible that Greek Cypriot authorities provided tacit permission for submarine operations in their maritime zones.
  • Such permission would violate the 1960 Treaty of Guarantee that established Cyprus's independence and the rights of Turkey, Greece, and the UK as guarantor powers.
  • Turkey views any Greek Cypriot military cooperation with Israel as a direct threat to its strategic position in the Eastern Mediterranean.

The Natanz Connection: Missile Trajectory

The eastward trajectory of the missiles, confirmed by the low-rising smoke trail climbing toward the east, traces a route over Syria and Iraq to reach Natanz in central Iran. This Mediterranean-launched vector offers several advantages:

  • Unexpected approach: Iran's air defenses are oriented primarily toward threats from the south (Gulf) and east. A Mediterranean-origin cruise missile arrives from the northwest, a less defended axis.
  • Syrian airspace: With the collapse of Syrian air sovereignty, the airspace over Syria provides an uncontested corridor for cruise missile transit.
  • Iraqi airspace: The U.S. maintains effective control over Iraqi airspace through its military presence, allowing missile overflight without interception.
  • Coordination: The submarine launch was timed to coincide with other strike platforms hitting Natanz simultaneously, creating a multi-axis attack that overwhelms Iranian defenses.

Iran's retaliatory strike on Dimona was explicitly linked to the Natanz attack, confirming that the submarine-launched missiles reached their target.

Erdogan's Dilemma: NATO Ally vs. Sovereignty

Turkey faces an impossible position:

  • As a NATO ally: Turkey is formally allied with the United States, the likely operator of the Virginia-class submarine. Treating the incident as an act of war against a NATO partner would fracture the alliance.
  • As a sovereign state: Allowing another country to use its territorial waters or adjacent waters as a launchpad for attacks on third countries sets a precedent that Turkey cannot accept.
  • As a regional power: Erdogan has positioned himself as a defender of the Muslim world against Israeli aggression. Being unable to detect or prevent Israel from launching missiles from his own backyard undermines this positioning entirely.
  • The detection gap: The most damaging aspect is not the diplomatic violation but the demonstrated inability of Turkey's military to detect a submarine operating within visual range of its coastline.

Conclusion: The Mediterranean Becomes a Launchpad

The submarine launch from waters between Turkey and Northern Cyprus transforms the Eastern Mediterranean into an active combat zone for the Iran war. The U.S. and Israel have demonstrated that they will use any body of water, regardless of whose sovereignty it abuts, as a platform for strikes on Iran.

For Turkey, the incident is both a diplomatic humiliation and a military wake-up call. The country that operates NATO's second-largest armed forces could not detect a submarine launching missiles from waters that fishermen can reach in a rowboat. For Iran, the multi-axis nature of the attack, with missiles arriving from the Mediterranean, the Gulf, and Israeli territory simultaneously, confirms that the entire region has been mobilized as a strike platform.

The submarine has departed. The sovereignty violation remains. And the Erdogan-Netanyahu confrontation, already volatile, has been pushed closer to a breaking point.

The smoke trail rose at a low angle before climbing eastward, consistent with a cruise missile trajectory over Syria and Iraq toward Iran. The timing of the launch coincided precisely with the strikes on Natanz reported earlier in the day, confirming that the submarine served as one of the launch platforms for the attack on Iran's primary uranium enrichment facility.

Virginia Class or Dolphin-2: The Identity Question

Turkish and regional intelligence agencies are working to determine whether the submarine was American or Israeli:

The Virginia-Class Hypothesis (U.S.)

  • A Virginia-class nuclear-powered attack submarine (SSN) from the USS Gerald R. Ford carrier strike group is known to be operating in the Eastern Mediterranean.
  • The submarine did not transit the Suez Canal with the carrier group and remained in the Eastern Mediterranean.
  • The Karpasia peninsula's underwater geography has been identified by U.S. naval planners as suitable for submarine operations targeting Iran from the Mediterranean vector.
  • The stealth capabilities of a nuclear submarine would explain why Turkish radars and coast guard patrols failed to detect the vessel.

The Dolphin-2 Hypothesis (Israel)

  • Israel's Dolphin-2 class submarines are diesel-electric vessels built in Germany, equipped with torpedo tubes capable of launching cruise missiles.
  • According to U.S. documents, all Israeli Dolphin-class submarines are currently deployed outside Israeli territorial waters.
  • 99% of Israeli submarines are operating beyond their home waters, dispersed across the Mediterranean and potentially the Indian Ocean.
  • The Dolphin-2 could have launched Popeye Turbo SLCM cruise missiles with sufficient range to reach Natanz via a Syria-Iraq flight path.

The prevailing assessment is that both platforms may have been involved: a Virginia-class providing the primary strike capability while a Dolphin-2 operated in coordination.

The Provocation: Erdogan's Warning and Netanyahu's Answer

The submarine launch was a direct response to President Erdogan's recent statement at a public gathering:

"The Middle East is boiling now. Zionist Israel has committed massacres against hundreds of thousands of people, and I have no doubt it will pay the price for this."

Netanyahu's answer came not in words but in action: launching missiles from waters adjacent to Turkish sovereign territory, demonstrating that Israel can project force through Turkey's sphere of influence without detection or permission.

The message to Erdogan is threefold:

  1. Your territorial waters are permeable: Turkish naval surveillance failed to detect the submarine before, during, or after the launch.
  2. Your F-16s arrived too late: By the time Turkey scrambled fighters, the submarine and its missiles were gone.
  3. Your threats have no operational backing: If Turkey cannot detect a submarine in its own coastal waters, its military threats against Israel lack credibility.

Turkey's Detection Failure: The Stealth Gap

The incident exposed a critical vulnerability in Turkey's naval surveillance architecture:

  • Radar failure: Neither coastal radars nor naval surveillance systems detected the submarine's approach, presence, or departure.
  • Coast guard blind: Turkish coast guard patrols in the area between Turkey and Northern Cyprus did not identify the submarine or its launch preparations.
  • Sonar gap: Turkey's anti-submarine warfare capabilities in the Eastern Mediterranean proved insufficient to detect a modern submarine operating in stealth mode.
  • Discovery by fishermen: The launch was first detected not by the Turkish military but by civilian fishermen who filmed the missile exhaust plume, a humiliating revelation for NATO's second-largest military.

Turkey has deployed F-16 fighters to Northern Cyprus and initiated a search for the submarine, but military analysts assess that the vessel has already withdrawn to deeper Mediterranean waters beyond Turkish detection range.

The Sovereignty Violation: International Law

The legal dimensions of the incident are severe regardless of whether the submarine operated in territorial or international waters:

If launched from Turkish/Northern Cyprus territorial waters:

  • This constitutes a direct violation of Turkish sovereignty under international law.
  • The use of another state's territorial waters to launch an attack on a third country is an act of belligerence that implicates the territorial state.
  • Turkey would have legal grounds to treat this as an act of war.

If launched from international waters between Turkey and Northern Cyprus:

  • Even from international waters, launching cruise missiles in close proximity to Turkish military bases (including the Turkish naval facility at Famagusta) represents a hostile act.
  • The flight path of the missiles over or near Turkish-controlled airspace adds an additional sovereignty concern.
  • The U.S. and Israel effectively treated the waters around Cyprus as if they were under their own sovereignty, as Turkish media noted.

Northern Cyprus's Presidential Media Center initially issued a statement claiming that reports of missiles launched from within its territorial waters "do not correspond to reality," a denial that Ankara pressured Nicosia to make despite the video evidence filmed from multiple angles by fishermen.

The Greek Cyprus Angle: Base Access Questions

The involvement of Greek Cypriot territory adds another layer of complexity:

  • Greek Cyprus hosts British Sovereign Base Areas (Akrotiri and Dhekelia) that have been used for Western military operations in the region.
  • It is possible that Greek Cypriot authorities provided tacit permission for submarine operations in their maritime zones.
  • Such permission would violate the 1960 Treaty of Guarantee that established Cyprus's independence and the rights of Turkey, Greece, and the UK as guarantor powers.
  • Turkey views any Greek Cypriot military cooperation with Israel as a direct threat to its strategic position in the Eastern Mediterranean.

The Natanz Connection: Missile Trajectory

The eastward trajectory of the missiles, confirmed by the low-rising smoke trail climbing toward the east, traces a route over Syria and Iraq to reach Natanz in central Iran. This Mediterranean-launched vector offers several advantages:

  • Unexpected approach: Iran's air defenses are oriented primarily toward threats from the south (Gulf) and east. A Mediterranean-origin cruise missile arrives from the northwest, a less defended axis.
  • Syrian airspace: With the collapse of Syrian air sovereignty, the airspace over Syria provides an uncontested corridor for cruise missile transit.
  • Iraqi airspace: The U.S. maintains effective control over Iraqi airspace through its military presence, allowing missile overflight without interception.
  • Coordination: The submarine launch was timed to coincide with other strike platforms hitting Natanz simultaneously, creating a multi-axis attack that overwhelms Iranian defenses.

Iran's retaliatory strike on Dimona was explicitly linked to the Natanz attack, confirming that the submarine-launched missiles reached their target.

Erdogan's Dilemma: NATO Ally vs. Sovereignty

Turkey faces an impossible position:

  • As a NATO ally: Turkey is formally allied with the United States, the likely operator of the Virginia-class submarine. Treating the incident as an act of war against a NATO partner would fracture the alliance.
  • As a sovereign state: Allowing another country to use its territorial waters or adjacent waters as a launchpad for attacks on third countries sets a precedent that Turkey cannot accept.
  • As a regional power: Erdogan has positioned himself as a defender of the Muslim world against Israeli aggression. Being unable to detect or prevent Israel from launching missiles from his own backyard undermines this positioning entirely.
  • The detection gap: The most damaging aspect is not the diplomatic violation but the demonstrated inability of Turkey's military to detect a submarine operating within visual range of its coastline.

Conclusion: The Mediterranean Becomes a Launchpad

The submarine launch from waters between Turkey and Northern Cyprus transforms the Eastern Mediterranean into an active combat zone for the Iran war. The U.S. and Israel have demonstrated that they will use any body of water, regardless of whose sovereignty it abuts, as a platform for strikes on Iran.

For Turkey, the incident is both a diplomatic humiliation and a military wake-up call. The country that operates NATO's second-largest armed forces could not detect a submarine launching missiles from waters that fishermen can reach in a rowboat. For Iran, the multi-axis nature of the attack, with missiles arriving from the Mediterranean, the Gulf, and Israeli territory simultaneously, confirms that the entire region has been mobilized as a strike platform.

The submarine has departed. The sovereignty violation remains. And the Erdogan-Netanyahu confrontation, already volatile, has been pushed closer to a breaking point.

item.title: Telegraph Leak: Mojtaba Khamenei’s Narrow Escape
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing the Telegraph's leaked audio from Mazhar Hosseini detailing the February 18 strike killing Ali Khamenei and Mojtaba's narrow escape.
item.content:encoded:
Telegraph Leak: Mojtaba Khamenei’s Narrow Escape

A leaked audio recording obtained and verified by the British newspaper The Daily Telegraph has provided the first detailed account of the U.S.-Israeli missile strike targeting the Supreme Leader's compound in Tehran on February 18, 2026. The recording, capturing remarks by Mazhar Hosseini, the Head of Protocol at the Leader's Office, reveals the scale of the casualties—including the death of Ali Khamenei and senior military commanders—and details how the newly elected Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, narrowly escaped assassination.

The Leaked Audio: Mazhar Hosseini’s Qolhak Briefing

The audio recording was captured during a private meeting held on March 2, 2026, in the Qolhak neighborhood of northern Tehran. Speaking before a gathering of senior clerics and IRGC officers, Mazhar Hosseini delivered a detailed briefing on the events inside the compound during the bombardment.

The verification of this recording by intelligence analysts confirms its authenticity. The leak represents a security breach within the clerical leadership, exposing details of the strike that Iranian state media had kept under strict censorship.

The February 18 Strike: Bombarding the Supreme Leader’s Compound

According to the briefing, the strike occurred at 11:32 AM local time on February 18, 2026. U.S. and Israeli forces launched a coordinated barrage of heavy bunker-buster missiles targeting the central residential and administrative offices of the Supreme Leader in Tehran.

The missiles targeted three separate structures within the compound simultaneously. The objective was to eliminate the entire leadership family and its close military advisors, leaving no immediate succession candidate to manage the state's command loop.

High-Command Casualties: Pakpour, Nasirzadeh, and Shirazi

The simultaneous impacts killed several of Iran's top military and defense officials who were attending a crisis meeting with the Supreme Leader. The casualties included:

  • Ali Khamenei: The Supreme Leader of the Republic.
  • Mohammad Pakpour: Commander of the IRGC Ground Forces.
  • Aziz Nasirzadeh: Minister of Defense.
  • Mohammad Shirazi: Chief of the Military Office of the Supreme Leader.

The deaths of these officials decapitated the defense establishment, forcing the remaining IRGC command to restructure their communication networks during active operations.

The Seizure of the Military Link: Targeting Mohammad Shirazi

The inclusion of General Mohammad Shirazi on the target list was strategic. Shirazi served as the vital coordinator between the Supreme Leader and the various branches of the armed forces, intelligence agencies, and the IRGC.

Western intelligence estimated that Shirazi would play a key role in managing the transition of power. The strike on his office was so severe that, according to Hosseini, only a few kilograms of remains were recovered to identify his body, disrupting the transition loop.

Mojtaba Khamenei’s Escape: Courtyard Walk and Minor Injury

The leaked recording reveals that Mojtaba Khamenei, who has since been elected as the new Supreme Leader, survived the strike due to a last-minute movement. Minutes before the missiles struck, Mojtaba stepped out of his upper-floor apartment into the courtyard to attend to a minor task.

As he was heading back inside, a missile struck his residence, destroying the structure. His wife and son were killed instantly in the blast, while Mojtaba suffered only a minor leg injury. His brother, Mostafa Khamenei, and his wife also survived a separate strike on a third residence, escaping from the rubble with minor injuries.

The Strategic Objective: Dismantling the Basij Command Loop

Beyond targeting the Khamenei family line, the strike aimed to neutralize Mojtaba's personal power base. Mojtaba has long held influence over the Basij paramilitary forces, having previously coordinated their internal security operations.

U.S. and Israeli planners targeted the Basij command structure, aiming to eliminate up to 300 regional commanders. By neutralizing the Basij leadership, coalition planners hoped to weaken the domestic security apparatus, allowing civil protests to challenge the regime. Mojtaba's survival prevented this vacuum, allowing him to consolidate Basij control.

Conclusion: The Security Isolation of the Khamenei Line

The details revealed by the leaked audio highlight the intensity of the U.S.-Israeli targeting campaign. By executing a simultaneous bunker-buster strike on the supreme command, the coalition demonstrated its intelligence access within the capital.

As Mojtaba Khamenei assumes the role of Supreme Leader under strict security protocols, the limits of his public appearances are clear. The necessity of hiding his physical location and modifying all audio and visual releases indicates that the leadership continues to operate under persistent threat, with security remaining the priority for the new administration.

item.title: Strategic Ambiguity Broken: Trump Confirms Israel’s Nukes
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing Donald Trump's speech breaking Israel's strategic nuclear ambiguity, David Sacks' warning, and the regional shift to proliferation.
item.content:encoded:
Strategic Ambiguity Broken: Trump Confirms Israel’s Nukes

U.S. President Donald Trump has broken the decades-old policy of "strategic ambiguity" regarding Israel's nuclear arsenal. During a public address on Monday night, Trump responded directly to questions concerning Israel's potential use of nuclear weapons in the conflict with Iran, confirming the existence of the arsenal while downplaying the likelihood of its deployment. The disclosure has prompted a reassessment of security doctrines across the Middle East.

The Monday Night Address: Breaking Decades of Ambiguity

During his speech, Donald Trump defended the U.S. military role in the Middle East, criticizing non-participating allies and outlining the scale of U.S. strikes. However, the focus of the address shifted during the question-and-answer session.

A journalist asked Trump to respond to warnings from his advisor, David Sacks, who suggested that further escalation could prompt Israel to utilize its nuclear weapons. Trump replied: "Yes, absolutely, but Israel will never do something like that. Israel will never do it." By addressing the topic directly, Trump confirmed the existence of Israel's nuclear capability, ending the policy of strategic silence maintained by successive U.S. administrations.

David Sacks’ Assessment: Declaring Victory to Avoid Escalation

The warning referenced by the journalist was published by political commentator and Trump advisor David Sacks. Sacks argued that the U.S. should "declare victory and withdraw" from the conflict with Iran.

Sacks warned that if the war continues to expand, Israel might consider the use of tactical nuclear weapons to secure its existence. Sacks suggested that since U.S. strikes had degraded Iran's infrastructure, withdrawing now would minimize the risk of a regional nuclear escalation, an assessment Trump acknowledged but bypassed in favor of continuing operations.

Strategic Ambiguity: The End of Israel’s Nuclear Taboo

Since the development of the Negev Nuclear Research Center in Dimona, Israel has maintained a policy of strategic ambiguity, neither confirming nor denying the possession of nuclear weapons. This policy allowed Israel to maintain a deterrent without triggering regional proliferation.

Trump's statement has altered this status. By acknowledging that Israel possesses these weapons but will "never use them," the U.S. president has normalized the discussion of Israel's nuclear status. This change limits the effectiveness of the ambiguity doctrine and forces regional states to adjust their defense planning.

The Proliferation Lesson: North Korea vs. the Iranian Model

The disclosure has highlighted a strategic lesson for non-nuclear states in the region. Analysts argue that the U.S. decision to attack Iran—beginning with the bombardment of Kharg Island—was made only after verifying that Iran did not possess a completed nuclear weapon.

In contrast, the possession of actual nuclear weapons has protected North Korea from Western military intervention. This difference illustrates the political philosophy of Thomas Hobbes, who argued that power must be demonstrated to be effective. For regional powers like Turkey and Iran, the lesson is clear: conventional defenses are insufficient to prevent intervention, and nuclear weaponization is the only reliable guarantee of security.

Infiltrating the Iranian Program: The Decision to Attack

The decision by U.S. and Israeli planners to launch the air campaign against Iran was based on intelligence access. Israeli intelligence had verified that Iran's enrichment remained at the 60% level (stored as Uranium Hexafluoride gas) and had not been converted to weapons-grade material.

Had there been a risk that Iran possessed a hidden nuclear warhead, the U.S. would have hesitated to launch strikes. The confirmation that Iran lacked a nuclear deterrent made the country a viable target for conventional intervention, proving that stopping short of weaponization does not prevent conflict.

The U.S. Trap: Israel’s Nuclear Weapons as Foreign Policy Leverage

The existence of Israel's nuclear weapons also influences U.S. foreign policy. Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended U.S. intervention by arguing that if the U.S. did not act, Israel would strike Iran unilaterally, leading to a regional war.

This dynamic creates a policy trap for Washington. By utilizing the threat of unilateral nuclear escalation, Israel can compel the U.S. to participate in regional operations. The U.S. is forced to support Israeli operations to prevent the deployment of tactical nuclear weapons, locking U.S. resources into regional conflicts.

Conclusion: The Shift Toward Regional Nuclear Proliferation

Trump's disclosure of Israel's nuclear weapons has changed the security calculations for the Middle East. By confirming the existence of the arsenal while demonstrating that non-nuclear states like Iran remain vulnerable to intervention, the U.S. has reduced the incentive for regional states to rely on conventional defense.

As regional powers assess the results of the air campaign, the pressure to develop nuclear deterrents is likely to increase. The breakdown of strategic ambiguity suggests that the future of Middle East security will be defined by nuclear proliferation, as nations conclude that acquiring these weapons is the only way to secure their sovereignty.

item.title: Trump Warns NATO Over Hormuz: Join Us or Face End
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing Donald Trump's warning to NATO over the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's targeting of Italian, French, and British military assets.
item.content:encoded:
Trump Warns NATO Over Hormuz: Join Us or Face End

U.S. President Donald Trump has warned that the NATO alliance faces a "very bad future" if European allies fail to assist the United States in reopening the Strait of Hormuz. In an 8-minute phone interview with the Financial Times, Trump urged European capitals to deploy minesweepers and special forces to secure the shipping lane. The warning comes as Iran systematically targets European military assets in the region—including Italian, French, and British forces—to deter them from joining the coalition.

The Financial Times Call: Trump’s Warning to NATO

Speaking directly to the Financial Times, Donald Trump expressed deep frustration with the reluctance of European allies to join the military effort against Iran. He criticized the asymmetry in the alliance's commitments, noting that while the U.S. provided billions of dollars in military aid to Ukraine, European nations are refusing to assist the U.S. in the Gulf.

Trump stated: "We have an alliance called NATO. We have been very generous to them. We didn't have to help them in Ukraine. Ukraine is thousands of miles away, but we helped them. Now we will see if they will help us. I have always said NATO is a one-way street, and if they don't respond, it will be very bad for the future of the alliance."

The Economic Stranglehold: Soaring Oil Prices and Closed Straits

The closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran, following the outbreak of hostilities two weeks ago, has triggered an energy crisis. Oil prices reached $106 per barrel, representing a 45% increase since the beginning of the war.

Trump acknowledged that the closure has severely impacted global supply chains. He argued that because Europe and China depend heavily on Gulf oil—unlike the energy-independent United States—it is only logical that they contribute naval assets to reopen the strait. The U.S. has requested the deployment of European minesweepers and commandos to clear Iranian sea mines and secure coastal sectors.

Friction with the UK: Keir Starmer’s Posture Dilemma

During the phone call, Trump expressed irritation with the response of UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer. According to Trump, Starmer initially refused to commit Royal Navy ships during the active phase of the operations, offering to send two vessels only after the U.S. had already degraded Iran's primary coastal defense batteries.

Starmer has maintained that the UK will limit its forces to a "defensive posture," refusing to expand naval operations from the Red Sea to the Strait of Hormuz. This caution is shared by other European capitals, which fear that joining the U.S. coalition will draw them into an all-out war with Iran.

The Beijing Summit Leverage: Pressuring China on Oil

As part of his diplomatic campaign, Trump hinted at delaying his scheduled summit in Beijing with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The trip, intended to cement a trade and technology truce, was scheduled for the end of the month.

Trump stated that China must assist in reopening the shipping corridor, noting that Beijing imports 90% of its oil through the Strait of Hormuz. By threatening to postpone the summit, Trump aims to leverage Beijing's economic dependence on the Gulf to force them to pressure Iran, though Chinese officials have shown no desire to delay the talks.

Iran’s Retaliatory Message to Italy: Kuwait Base Struck

To prevent European nations from joining the U.S. coalition, Iran has launched targeted strikes against European military assets in the Middle East. Official military statements in Kuwait confirmed that an Iranian drone strike completely incinerated an Italian strategic surveillance drone parked at a local airbase.

This strike follows a previous Shahed drone attack on March 11-12, 2026, which targeted the Italian military contingent at Camp Singara in Erbil, Iraqi Kurdistan. While the 300 Italian soldiers stationed at the camp suffered no casualties, the attack caused significant damage to logistics and equipment, sending a clear warning to Rome.

Targeting French Operatives and British Cyprus Bases

The Iranian retaliation campaign has also targeted French and British forces:

  • France: Iranian news agency Tasnim reported a surgical strike against a French intelligence and special operations cell in Erbil. The cell was accused of coordinating operations with Iranian Kurdish groups. The strike killed one French officer and wounded five others.
  • United Kingdom: Tehran has targeted the two British military bases in Cyprus (Akrotiri and Dhekelia) with drone salvos. The IRGC warned London that any British participation in intercepting Iranian missiles or refueling U.S. bombers would lead to direct strikes on the Cyprus bases.

Conclusion: The Isolation of the Coalition Powers

Trump's warning to NATO and his appeals to China demonstrate the limitations of unilateral U.S. power projection in the Gulf. By systematically targeting Italian, French, and British assets on the ground, Iran has successfully raised the costs of participation for European capitals, leaving the U.S. and Israel isolated.

As oil prices continue to rise and European leaders refuse to commit commandos, the U.S. administration's options for reopening the Strait of Hormuz are narrowing. The breakdown of the coalition suggests that the conflict is accelerating the shift toward a multipolar Middle East, where Western security guarantees are no longer sufficient to secure global energy corridors.

The closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran, following the outbreak of hostilities two weeks ago, has triggered an energy crisis. Oil prices reached $106 per barrel, representing a 45% increase since the beginning of the war.

Trump acknowledged that the closure has severely impacted global supply chains. He argued that because Europe and China depend heavily on Gulf oil—unlike the energy-independent United States—it is only logical that they contribute naval assets to reopen the strait. The U.S. has requested the deployment of European minesweepers and commandos to clear Iranian sea mines and secure coastal sectors.

Friction with the UK: Keir Starmer’s Posture Dilemma

During the phone call, Trump expressed irritation with the response of UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer. According to Trump, Starmer initially refused to commit Royal Navy ships during the active phase of the operations, offering to send two vessels only after the U.S. had already degraded Iran's primary coastal defense batteries.

Starmer has maintained that the UK will limit its forces to a "defensive posture," refusing to expand naval operations from the Red Sea to the Strait of Hormuz. This caution is shared by other European capitals, which fear that joining the U.S. coalition will draw them into an all-out war with Iran.

The Beijing Summit Leverage: Pressuring China on Oil

As part of his diplomatic campaign, Trump hinted at delaying his scheduled summit in Beijing with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The trip, intended to cement a trade and technology truce, was scheduled for the end of the month.

Trump stated that China must assist in reopening the shipping corridor, noting that Beijing imports 90% of its oil through the Strait of Hormuz. By threatening to postpone the summit, Trump aims to leverage Beijing's economic dependence on the Gulf to force them to pressure Iran, though Chinese officials have shown no desire to delay the talks.

Iran’s Retaliatory Message to Italy: Kuwait Base Struck

To prevent European nations from joining the U.S. coalition, Iran has launched targeted strikes against European military assets in the Middle East. Official military statements in Kuwait confirmed that an Iranian drone strike completely incinerated an Italian strategic surveillance drone parked at a local airbase.

This strike follows a previous Shahed drone attack on March 11-12, 2026, which targeted the Italian military contingent at Camp Singara in Erbil, Iraqi Kurdistan. While the 300 Italian soldiers stationed at the camp suffered no casualties, the attack caused significant damage to logistics and equipment, sending a clear warning to Rome.

Targeting French Operatives and British Cyprus Bases

The Iranian retaliation campaign has also targeted French and British forces:

  • France: Iranian news agency Tasnim reported a surgical strike against a French intelligence and special operations cell in Erbil. The cell was accused of coordinating operations with Iranian Kurdish groups. The strike killed one French officer and wounded five others.
  • United Kingdom: Tehran has targeted the two British military bases in Cyprus (Akrotiri and Dhekelia) with drone salvos. The IRGC warned London that any British participation in intercepting Iranian missiles or refueling U.S. bombers would lead to direct strikes on the Cyprus bases.

Conclusion: The Isolation of the Coalition Powers

Trump's warning to NATO and his appeals to China demonstrate the limitations of unilateral U.S. power projection in the Gulf. By systematically targeting Italian, French, and British assets on the ground, Iran has successfully raised the costs of participation for European capitals, leaving the U.S. and Israel isolated.

As oil prices continue to rise and European leaders refuse to commit commandos, the U.S. administration's options for reopening the Strait of Hormuz are narrowing. The breakdown of the coalition suggests that the conflict is accelerating the shift toward a multipolar Middle East, where Western security guarantees are no longer sufficient to secure global energy corridors.

item.title: Oil Diplomacy: The Secret Trump-Putin Deal on Iran
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing the secret Trump-Putin phone call, the G7 oil reserve intervention, and Israel's alternative economic axis linking Azerbaijan, India, and Greece.
item.content:encoded:
Oil Diplomacy: The Secret Trump-Putin Deal on Iran

The convergence of military escalation in the Persian Gulf and shifting global oil prices has triggered intense backchannel diplomacy. Facing mounting domestic pressure to lower fuel prices, U.S. President Donald Trump initiated a crucial phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin. This conversation has laid the groundwork for a potential grand bargain, connecting regional settlements in both Ukraine and Iran to stabilize global energy markets.

The Secret Call: Trump’s Oil Price Challenge

With domestic polls indicating that 67% of Americans anticipate rising gasoline prices, and only 29% supporting the ongoing military campaign in the Middle East, the U.S. administration faced a political emergency. To cool the market, Trump contacted Russian President Vladimir Putin.

During the call, the two leaders discussed a coordinated de-escalation plan. In exchange for Russian mediation with Iran and assistance in stabilizing oil prices, Trump signaled a willingness to offer concessions to Moscow regarding the conflict in Ukraine. The proposal, a 6-point plan drafted in coordination with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, aims to establish a joint framework for ceasefires in both theatres.

Market Volatility: The Brent Crude Rollercoaster

The impact of the conflict on energy markets has been highly volatile. On Monday, Brent crude surged by nearly 30%, peaking at $119.50 per barrel, its highest level in three years, driven by threats to shipping in the Persian Gulf.

However, following news of the Trump-Putin call and coordinated G7 announcements, prices fell by more than 10% the following day, dropping below $89.85 per barrel. Analysts indicate that this rapid fluctuation reflects the market's sensitivity to political interventions, oscillating between fears of a total energy blockade and hopes for a negotiated settlement.

Coordinated Interventions: G7 and IEA Strategic Reserves

To counter price increases, the United States coordinated a joint response with the Group of Seven (G7) and the International Energy Agency (IEA). The coalition threatened to release massive strategic petroleum reserves to flood the market and offset any supply deficits.

U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright reassured markets that the price spikes would be temporary, citing record U.S. domestic production and abundant global supplies. These assurances, combined with predictions that shipping through the Strait of Hormuz would gradually normalize, helped cool speculative trading and stabilize contract prices.

Iran’s Economic Warfare and Ceasefire Redlines

Iran's military strategy has focused on leveraging its position in energy markets to force an end to the war. The IRGC previously threatened to block all transit through the Strait of Hormuz, which handles approximately 20 million barrels of oil per day.

However, once Trump signaled an accelerated timeline for ending operations—claiming in a CNBC interview that the military campaign was ahead of schedule—Tehran clarified its position. Iranian officials stated that if U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iranian infrastructure cease, Iran will halt its retaliatory strikes, preferring a frozen conflict over continued economic escalation.

The Strait of Hormuz Threat and OPEC Production Cuts

The threat to the Strait of Hormuz remains a primary concern for energy analysts. A prolonged blockade of this vital maritime chokepoint could lead to severe disruptions in global supply chains.

These concerns are compounded by significant production cuts among Gulf producers. Saudi Arabia has reduced output by 2 to 2.5 million barrels per day, Iraq by 2.9 million, the UAE by 500,000 to 800,000, and Kuwait by 500,000. These cuts, totaling approximately 6.7 million barrels per day (about a third of their combined capacity), have limited the market's spare capacity, making it vulnerable to supply disruptions.

Israel’s Alternative Axis: Sidelining Turkey

To protect its economy from maritime blockades and shipping disruptions, Israel has developed an alternative trade and supply network. This system relies on a strategic quad-alliance:

  1. Azerbaijan: Supplies 100% of the crude oil needed for Israeli domestic consumption and military operations.
  2. Greece: Absorbs transit costs and secures shipping routes through the eastern Mediterranean.
  3. Ethiopia: Serves as a logistical air hub, receiving international cargo and flying it directly to Israeli airports.
  4. India: Acts as a key partner for manufacturing, technology, and industrial components.

This network has sidelined Turkey's President Erdogan, who had expected to position Turkey as a key intermediary under the Trump administration, only to see Washington support this alternative axis.

Conclusion: The Geopolitical Price of Crude

The fluctuations in global energy markets highlight the connection between geopolitics and commodity prices. While military operations can drive rapid price increases, backchannel diplomacy and coordinated reserve releases can stabilize markets.

As negotiations continue, the strategic balance remains delicate. The U.S. administration aims to conclude its operations quickly to prevent domestic economic backlash, while Israel seeks to isolate Iran from international markets. The outcome of the Trump-Putin negotiations will determine whether the region transitions toward a negotiated ceasefire or continues to experience localized energy shocks.

item.title: Trump Rejects Gulf Ceasefire as Iran Shifts to Clusters
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Trump rejects Qatar-UAE ceasefire initiative. Iran redirects 70% cluster warheads toward Israel. IDF Chief Zamiri admits war is not halfway through.
item.content:encoded:
Trump Rejects Gulf Ceasefire as Iran Shifts to Clusters

President Trump has rejected a joint Qatari-Emirati ceasefire initiative, backed quietly by Saudi Arabia, declaring that a halt to operations is "not on the table." In the same 24-hour window, Iran doubled its missile launch rate against Israel to 20 missiles per day, with 70% carrying cluster warheads designed for maximum area damage. IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamiri stated publicly that "we have not even reached the halfway point," while Israeli Channel 12 called it the hardest day of the war. The convergence of diplomatic rejection, escalating firepower, and a promised U.S. ground operation on Kharg Island signals that this conflict is entering a new and more dangerous phase.

The Gulf Ceasefire Initiative: Qatar and UAE Move

Emir Tamim of Qatar and President Mohammed bin Zayed of the UAE launched a coordinated diplomatic initiative to halt the war immediately. The proposal, supported by contacts with the Russian leadership, called for an immediate ceasefire and negotiations under fire, a framework that Iran indicated it could accept.

The initiative represented a significant break from the Gulf states' earlier posture. Both Qatar and the UAE had been targeted by Iranian retaliatory strikes on their energy infrastructure, giving them direct motivation to end the conflict. Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, while not formally joining the initiative, were waiting for its success before attaching their names.

Trump's Rejection: "Not on the Table"

Trump dismissed the Gulf initiative outright, siding instead with IDF Chief Zamiri's assessment that the war must continue. This rejection carries several implications:

  • Gulf allies humiliated: Qatar and the UAE invested significant diplomatic capital, including Russian coordination, only to be publicly overruled.
  • Saudi and Kuwaiti bases remain active: Trump reinforced operations at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait and Prince Sultan Air Base (Al Kharj) in Saudi Arabia, signaling that these countries remain operational platforms regardless of their diplomatic preferences.
  • Zamiri over Trump's own timeline: Trump had previously claimed the war would set Iran back ten years. Zamiri publicly contradicted this, stating the damage amounts to eight months of capacity, and that without continuation, Israel would face another round within a year. Trump accepted Zamiri's assessment over his own.

Iran Strikes Aviation Fuel Depots in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia

In a direct operational response to the Gulf states' failure to secure a ceasefire, Iran struck aviation fuel storage depots at both Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait and Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia. These strikes targeted the critical logistics chain: without jet fuel, the U.S. and Israeli air campaigns cannot sustain their sortie rates.

The strikes serve a dual purpose. Militarily, they degrade the operational capacity of forward-deployed air wings. Politically, they punish Kuwait and Saudi Arabia for continuing to host U.S. strike operations despite the diplomatic push for peace. The message to Riyadh and Kuwait City is clear: hosting American operations makes your infrastructure a legitimate target.

The 70% Cluster Shift: Fewer Warheads, Greater Destruction

Israeli defense sources, confirmed by security correspondent Eyal Zamir, revealed that 70% of Iranian missiles now carry cluster munitions. This represents a fundamental shift in Iran's targeting doctrine:

  • Cluster warheads: Each missile disperses fewer but larger submunitions, each capable of producing wider blast damage upon ground impact.
  • Area denial: Unlike precision strikes against point targets (refineries, radar stations), cluster munitions are designed to saturate large areas, maximizing casualties and infrastructure damage.
  • Psychological impact: Israeli Channel 12 described the current phase as "the hardest days of the war," driven by the shift from precision to area-effect weapons.

The Israeli military noted that while the individual submunition count per missile is lower than standard cluster configurations, each warhead is significantly larger, producing greater destructive force per impact point.

20 Missiles Per Day: The Redirect from Gulf to Israel

Iranian missile launches against Israel doubled to approximately 20 per day, roughly twice the rate of the previous phase. Israeli defense analysts attributed this increase to a deliberate redirect: Iran reduced its strikes on Gulf states and concentrated firepower on Israel.

Since the beginning of the war, Iran has conducted approximately 400 launch operations. The redirect toward Israel coincides with the Gulf ceasefire initiative, suggesting that Tehran is using the reduced pressure on the Gulf as leverage to encourage Qatar and the UAE to press harder for a diplomatic solution, while simultaneously punishing Israel for rejecting negotiations.

Zamiri's Admission: "Not Even Halfway"

IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamiri's public statement that the war has not reached its midpoint is the most significant Israeli military assessment to date. The implications are severe:

  • Eight months of damage, not ten years: Zamiri confirmed that the combined U.S.-Israeli campaign has degraded Iranian military capacity by approximately eight months of production, far short of Trump's claim of a decade-long setback.
  • Another round inevitable: Israeli security sources stated that if the war stops now, Israel will face another confrontation with Iran within eight months to a year.
  • Continuation imperative: The Israeli military establishment is pushing for extended operations, including a naval and air blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and the Caspian Sea, estimating that control of Hormuz and Kharg Island would take approximately two weeks.

Trump's Promise: A Ground Operation on Kharg Island

The most consequential development is Trump's reported promise to Netanyahu: a joint ground operation targeting Kharg Island and the Iranian coastline to break Tehran's control over the Strait of Hormuz. This represents the maximum escalation scenario.

The strategic logic is that a naval blockade combined with a ground seizure of Kharg, through which 90% of Iran's oil exports flow, would trigger an economic collapse that could bring down the Iranian government. In exchange, Trump agreed to Netanyahu's demand to avoid striking oil and gas infrastructure directly, focusing instead on industrial and missile manufacturing facilities.

The Israeli-Iranian Target Bank War

Both sides are now engaged in a parallel industrial targeting campaign:

  • Israel struck: Military-industrial facilities across Tehran and central Iran, including Industrial Zone C in Isfahan, where the IRGC Air Force commander was reportedly present.
  • Iran responded: With precision strikes against Israeli radar installations, satellite communication nodes, and the deputy chief of military intelligence, using Ghadr and Khaybar Shekan missiles in coordinated waves (Wave 9).
  • Israeli sortie reduction: Israeli air operations dropped by approximately 30% from previous phases due to Iranian strikes on radar and satellite communication infrastructure, forcing a target bank update from field-level intelligence rather than signals intelligence.

Gulf Realignment: Qatar and UAE Isolated

Trump's rejection of the ceasefire initiative has created a new dynamic among Gulf states:

  • Qatar and UAE: Diplomatically wounded, having coordinated with Russia and put their proposal on Trump's desk, only to be dismissed.
  • Saudi Arabia and Kuwait: Waiting on the sidelines, unwilling to formally join an initiative that Trump rejected, but increasingly uncomfortable with hosting operations that draw Iranian retaliation.
  • Russia: Supports the Gulf ceasefire initiative as part of its broader strategy to freeze Western operations in the Middle East.

The result is a potential isolation of Qatar and the UAE from the U.S.-Israeli war coalition, with both states potentially restricting base access or reducing logistical support as their own populations absorb the consequences of continued conflict.

Conclusion: The War Deepens

Trump's rejection of the Gulf ceasefire initiative, combined with Zamiri's admission that the war is far from over, signals that the conflict is entering its most intensive phase. Iran's shift to cluster warheads and the doubling of its missile rate against Israel indicate that Tehran is prepared to absorb losses while inflicting maximum damage. The promised ground operation on Kharg Island, if executed, would represent the largest U.S. amphibious operation since the 2003 invasion of Iraq, with consequences that could reshape the entire region.
