item.title: The Third Leader: Mojtaba Khamenei Emerges Amid War
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing the ascension of Sayyid Mojtaba Khamenei as Iran's third Supreme Leader, representing a failure of U.S., British, and Israeli plots.
item.content:encoded:
The Third Leader: Mojtaba Khamenei Ascends Amid War

In a historic and highly consequential development, the Iranian Assembly of Experts has officially announced the election of Sayyid Mojtaba Khamenei as the third Supreme Leader of the Islamic Republic of Iran. Choosing a hardline former Basij commander in the middle of an active conflict represents a major consolidation of power. The smooth succession has dealt a significant blow to U.S., British, and Israeli intelligence agencies, which had spent weeks attempting to disrupt the transition and force a collapse of the regime.

The Succession: Election of the Third Supreme Leader

The Assembly of Experts (مجلس خبراء القيادة) released a formal proclamation to the Iranian people, calling on them to pledge allegiance (Bay'ah) to Mojtaba Khamenei. According to Iran's constitution, Article 111 dictates the formation of a temporary leadership council in the event of a transition. However, to prevent any leadership vacuum during an active war, the Assembly bypassed this provision.

Following extensive closed-door deliberations, the Assembly selected Mojtaba Khamenei by an overwhelming, decisive majority of its members. The election positions Mojtaba to carry forward the legacy of Ruhollah Khomeini and his father, Ali Khamenei, ensuring ideological continuity at the highest level of state power.

Targeting the Succession: Bombing the Assembly’s Offices

The election was held under extreme security conditions. During the deliberations, Israeli airstrikes directly targeted the Secretariat General's offices of the Assembly of Experts in Tehran. The attack resulted in the deaths of several administrative staff and security personnel.

The strike was a direct attempt by Western and Israeli intelligence to physically disrupt the voting process and prevent the Assembly from selecting a successor. However, the Assembly refused to suspend its sessions, finalizing the selection of Mojtaba Khamenei and demonstrating the resilience of the regime's core administrative structures.

Failed Assassinations and the Ahmadinejad Alliance

Western intelligence agencies have long identified Mojtaba Khamenei as a primary obstacle to a diplomatic realignment. Over the past few weeks, Israeli operational teams launched at least three failed assassination attempts against him, alongside two major security breaches.

U.S. and Israeli strikes also targeted Mojtaba’s key political ally, former President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, striking his residence. Ahmadinejad, who remains alive, represents the populist conservative wing that partnered with Mojtaba during his leadership of the Basij forces. This political alliance has historically championed Iran’s nuclear program, and their consolidation ensures that the executive and clerical branches remain aligned under a hardline doctrine.

The Government-in-Exile: Israel’s Venezuela Strategy

As it became clear that Mojtaba Khamenei would succeed his father, Israel attempted to initiate a regime-change scenario. The Israeli Ambassador in Washington held meetings with leaders of the Iranian monarchist and liberal opposition to lay the groundwork for declaring a "government-in-exile."

This strategy mirrors the Venezuelan scenario (the Juan Guaidó model), attempting to bypass the clerical establishment and create a parallel government that Western nations could recognize. However, without active support on the ground and facing a highly mobilized Basij force, the strategy has failed to gain traction, serving only to solidify domestic support for the new Supreme Leader.

British Threats and the Cypriot Passport Asset

The U.S. and Israel were not alone in trying to block Mojtaba’s ascension. British intelligence launched a campaign linking Mojtaba to an investor named "Ansari," a Cypriot passport holder who allegedly managed financial networks and investments for the IRGC. London banned Ansari’s operations in a bid to freeze Mojtaba's financial channels.

Furthermore, Britain delivered a direct warning to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian: if Mojtaba Khamenei was elected, the UK would transition from defensive support to active offensive operations against Iran. This threat has pushed the UK and other European states to align more closely with U.S. bomber campaigns, allowing the U.S. to operate from British bases.

Strategic Consolidation: Failure of the Reformist Split

The election of Mojtaba Khamenei marks the failure of the Western strategy to exploit internal divisions between reformists and hardliners. Planners in Washington had hoped that the pressure of the war would force Pezeshkian's reformist government to break with the clerical establishment and seek a unilateral deal.

Instead, the military pressure has unified the entire political spectrum. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reiterated that Iran will not negotiate under pressure or in the shadow of war. Rather than dividing the country, the U.S. bomber campaign has forced the reformist presidency, the conservative parliament, and the IRGC into a single national defense front.

Conclusion: The Open-Ended Confrontation

Mojtaba Khamenei’s ascension has rewritten the parameters of the conflict. By electing a former commander of the Basij with deep ties to the security apparatus, Iran has signaled that it will not capitulate to U.S. or Israeli military pressure.

With Donald Trump warning that the new leader's reign will face constant opposition, the path to a quick diplomatic resolution has closed. The war is no longer a tactical standoff; it has become an open-ended confrontation between a unified Iranian leadership and a U.S.-led coalition, with both sides bracing for a long-term war of attrition.

item.title: Phase of Brutality: Segula Strike & Civilian Targets
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing the escalation of civilian targeting in Iran and the retaliatory Iranian cluster missile strike on the Segula industrial zone in Petah Tikva.
item.content:encoded:
Stage of Brutality: Segula Strike and Civilian Targets

The U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran has entered what the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) officially describes as a "stage of brutality." With strategic military options failing to dismantle the Iranian state, coalition forces have shifted their parameters to target vital civilian utilities—including power stations, refineries, and medical centers. In immediate retaliation, Iran launched a devastating cluster ballistic missile strike targeting the Segula industrial zone in Petah Tikva, bringing the realities of the war to the heart of Israel.

The Escalation to Brutality: Targeting Civilians

In the initial phases of the war, both sides claimed to focus strictly on military installations and command centers. However, as the conflict drags on, the strategic deadlock has forced a transition. Failing to trigger a popular uprising or collapse the government in Tehran, U.S. and Israeli air forces began targeting civilian infrastructure.

Over the past week, strikes have hit energy refineries, water desalination networks, and medical centers (such as kidney dialysis facilities) in cities like Shiraz, Isfahan, and Dezful. This campaign has resulted in over 1,000 civilian deaths in Iran, marking a qualitative shift in coalition tactics toward total economic and humanitarian pressure.

The Segula Cluster Strike: Petah Tikva Under Fire

Iran's response to the destruction of its civilian infrastructure was swift and highly destructive. Air raid sirens sounded across the Dan region, the coastal plain, and Samaria as Iranian ballistic missiles penetrated the air defense envelope.

A heavy cluster missile, designed to break apart into multiple warheads, detonated over the Segula industrial zone in Petah Tikva, in central Israel. The strike scattered submunitions across eight distinct sites within the industrial complex, causing massive fires and sending thick plumes of black smoke over the city. The attack triggered widespread panic, shattering the illusion of safety that Israel's air defense network had previously provided.

Emergency Mobilization: Command on the Ground

The scale of the Segula strike forced an immediate, high-level emergency response. As unexploded submunitions littered the industrial zone, police, fire crews, and search-and-rescue teams mobilized to secure the area and prevent secondary explosions.

High-ranking commanders rushed to the scene to coordinate the operations, including Major General Amir Cohen (Central/Sharon District Commander), Major General Eli Pinto, and Major General Aviad Katfi (Petah Tikva Police Chief). Their presence highlighted the severity of the security breach, as emergency services struggled to contain the fallout from a single cluster warhead that successfully bypassed defensive systems.

CENTCOM’s Strategic Reinterpretation of International Law

To justify this shift toward targeting residential and civilian-heavy areas, CENTCOM has introduced a controversial legal argument. U.S. military officials claim that because Iranian-aligned groups targeted U.S. military personnel housed in civilian hotels and private residential quarters throughout the Gulf, these civilian areas have lost their protected status.

Admiral Brad Cooper stated that by integrating military operations into civilian spheres, Iran has compromised the safety of its own people. This legal reinterpretation is seen by critics as a preemptive justification for expanding the target list to include residential zones, indicating that the coalition is prepared to tolerate much higher civilian casualties.

The Failure of the Decoy-Based Regime Change Theory

The shift to civilian targeting reveals a failure in the coalition's initial strategic assumptions. Western planners had hoped that destroying Iran's military capacity would leave the government weak and prompt the population to rise up.

However, because Iran successfully protected its core military assets through a massive decoy campaign, the coalition's first wave was largely ineffective. Left without immediate military targets to exploit, and facing mounting pressure from the White House, commanders shifted their focus to civilian infrastructure in a desperate attempt to force a political collapse.

Netanyahu’s Surprises: Systematic Utility Destruction

The systematic destruction of civilian infrastructure aligns with Benjamin Netanyahu's warnings of upcoming "surprises" in the war. These surprises are now visible: the targeting of domestic energy supplies, hospital facilities, and water distribution networks.

This strategy is supported by statements from Washington. Speaking on ABC, Donald Trump declared that the next Iranian leader would not survive without U.S. approval, claiming that the military campaign was necessary to prevent Iran from dominating the entire Middle East. This statement reinforces the coalition's commitment to forcing a complete political transition through economic destruction.

Conclusion: The Threat of Mutual Attrition

The strike on Petah Tikva is a warning of the consequences of targeting civilian populations. While the U.S. and Israel struggle to protect critical logistics at Al-Azraq Airbase in Jordan and various installations in the Gulf, Iran is proving that it can retaliate against Israel's industrial heartland.

As both sides expand their target lists to include civilian utilities, the war is turning into a campaign of mutual economic destruction. If the escalation continues, the resulting humanitarian crisis will spread far beyond Iran's borders, engulfing the entire region in an uncontrollable war of attrition.

item.title: War as a Facade: Trump, Netanyahu, and Epstein
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing how the U.S.-Israel confrontation with Iran serves as a political and legal shield for Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu.
item.content:encoded:
War as a Shield: Trump, Netanyahu, and the Epstein Cover-up

As the drums of war beat louder across the Persian Gulf, a critical question emerges: is the U.S.-Israeli escalation against Iran being used to cover up massive domestic scandals? Both Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu are facing severe legal crises that threaten their political survival. By aligning the deep state interests of both nations toward an existential regional war, both leaders are attempting to shield themselves from judicial accountability.

The Geopolitical Diversion: War as a Shield

In the realm of political economy, external conflicts are frequently utilized as diversionary tactics to mask domestic vulnerability. Today, the confrontation with Iran serves as a grand shield. For the Trump administration, a regional war aligns the interests of the Pentagon and intelligence agencies behind the presidency.

Similarly, for Netanyahu, maintaining state-of-emergency conditions keeps his government intact and prevents the resumption of judicial trials that could end his career. The geopolitical stakes are raised to an existential level, framing any domestic legal action against these leaders as an act of political sabotage.

The Epstein Scandal: FBI Files Unleashed

The domestic storm in Washington escalated following the release of heavily redacted FBI files by the Department of Justice (DOJ). The documents contain detailed testimonies from a victim alleging she was sexually assaulted by Donald Trump as a minor (between 13 and 15 years old), a meeting facilitated by Jeffrey Epstein.

The victim detailed specific incidents, including physical marks left during the assault, to verify her claims. The release of these files followed investigative reports by National Public Radio (NPR), which revealed that the DOJ had withheld these files under the guise of administrative duplication errors. Factions within the Democratic Party have labeled this a coordinated cover-up.

Political Firestorm: The House Judiciary Subpoena

The release of the Epstein files has triggered a massive legislative backlash. The House Judiciary Committee recently approved a formal subpoena for the U.S. Attorney General (referred to as the Minister of Justice). The Attorney General has been called to testify and deliver direct answers regarding the DOJ's handling and withholding of these sensitive files.

With allegations that Trump's circle used telephone threats and financial pressure to silence witnesses for years, the scandal presents a severe threat. For Democrats, the subpoena is a tool to expose systemic government corruption, while the administration frames it as a partisan weapon designed to obstruct the executive branch during a critical foreign conflict.

Pressuring Jerusalem: Trump’s Demands for Netanyahu's Pardon

At the same time, Trump is exerting pressure on the Israeli presidency. Reports indicate that Trump has directly pressured Israeli President Isaac Herzog to grant an immediate, preemptive pardon to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Netanyahu’s ongoing corruption trials in Israeli courts present a constant threat of imprisonment. Trump has argued that Herzog must issue a pardon so Netanyahu can focus entirely on the war against Iran without being distracted by legal proceedings. This interference in Israel’s independent judiciary has caused severe friction within Jerusalem's establishment, which rejects external directives on domestic legal procedures.

Herzog and Huckabee: Containment and Apology

The diplomatic fallout from Trump's pressure became public after he launched a direct attack on Isaac Herzog for refusing to commit to Netanyahu's pardon. To contain the damage, the U.S. Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, publicly defended Herzog, calling him one of the most critical allies of the United States.

Huckabee's public statement and subsequent meeting with Herzog served as an unofficial apology from Washington. However, the incident exposed a deeper reality: Trump's expectation of absolute obedience from regional leaders. While Trump claims Herzog previously promised to work on a pardon, Israeli officials have denied any such agreements.

Netanyahu's Long-Term Calculus: The Sparta Doctrine

Netanyahu’s cooperation with Trump is driven by a distinct long-term calculus. Factions within Netanyahu's coalition believe that the completion of the war against Iran will redefine Israel's regional status. The goal is to transform Israel into a militarized "Sparta"—a state that dominates the entire Middle East.

Under this doctrine, once regional adversaries are neutralized, Israel can achieve military and economic independence from U.S. financial aid. By utilizing the current window of U.S. support to destroy surrounding geopolitical threats, Netanyahu aims to secure his legacy as the leader who positioned Israel as the supreme regional hegemon.

Conclusion: The Interlocking Standoff

The domestic scandals in Washington and the judicial trials in Jerusalem are directly linked to the military escalation in the Middle East. The war against Iran is not merely a strategic choice; it is a mechanism for political survival.

As Congress pushes its investigation into the Epstein files and Israeli courts continue Netanyahu's trials, the temptation to expand the conflict remains high. Historically, when leaders are cornered by the rule of law at home, they look to the battlefield to rewrite their fate.

With allegations that Trump's circle used telephone threats and financial pressure to silence witnesses for years, the scandal presents a severe threat. For Democrats, the subpoena is a tool to expose systemic government corruption, while the administration frames it as a partisan weapon designed to obstruct the executive branch during a critical foreign conflict.

Pressuring Jerusalem: Trump’s Demands for Netanyahu's Pardon

At the same time, Trump is exerting pressure on the Israeli presidency. Reports indicate that Trump has directly pressured Israeli President Isaac Herzog to grant an immediate, preemptive pardon to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Netanyahu’s ongoing corruption trials in Israeli courts present a constant threat of imprisonment. Trump has argued that Herzog must issue a pardon so Netanyahu can focus entirely on the war against Iran without being distracted by legal proceedings. This interference in Israel’s independent judiciary has caused severe friction within Jerusalem's establishment, which rejects external directives on domestic legal procedures.

Herzog and Huckabee: Containment and Apology

The diplomatic fallout from Trump's pressure became public after he launched a direct attack on Isaac Herzog for refusing to commit to Netanyahu's pardon. To contain the damage, the U.S. Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, publicly defended Herzog, calling him one of the most critical allies of the United States.

Huckabee's public statement and subsequent meeting with Herzog served as an unofficial apology from Washington. However, the incident exposed a deeper reality: Trump's expectation of absolute obedience from regional leaders. While Trump claims Herzog previously promised to work on a pardon, Israeli officials have denied any such agreements.

Netanyahu's Long-Term Calculus: The Sparta Doctrine

Netanyahu’s cooperation with Trump is driven by a distinct long-term calculus. Factions within Netanyahu's coalition believe that the completion of the war against Iran will redefine Israel's regional status. The goal is to transform Israel into a militarized "Sparta"—a state that dominates the entire Middle East.

Under this doctrine, once regional adversaries are neutralized, Israel can achieve military and economic independence from U.S. financial aid. By utilizing the current window of U.S. support to destroy surrounding geopolitical threats, Netanyahu aims to secure his legacy as the leader who positioned Israel as the supreme regional hegemon.

Conclusion: The Interlocking Standoff

The domestic scandals in Washington and the judicial trials in Jerusalem are directly linked to the military escalation in the Middle East. The war against Iran is not merely a strategic choice; it is a mechanism for political survival.

As Congress pushes its investigation into the Epstein files and Israeli courts continue Netanyahu's trials, the temptation to expand the conflict remains high. Historically, when leaders are cornered by the rule of law at home, they look to the battlefield to rewrite their fate.

item.title: Blinded Skies: US Launches Major Bomber Campaign
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Investigating the U.S. transition to a heavy bomber campaign after Iran successfully neutralized MQ-9 and U-2 assets at Al Dhafra base.
item.content:encoded:
Blinded Skies: US Launches Phase Two Heavy Bomber Campaign

A significant military escalation has unfolded in the Middle East. Deprived of critical intelligence assets due to highly successful Iranian counter-reconnaissance operations, the United States has launched a massive "Phase Two" heavy bomber campaign. With high-altitude surveillance networks severely disrupted, Washington is shifting from precision tactical fighter strikes to heavy strategic bombardment in an attempt to reset the geopolitical balance of power.

Blinding the Eyes: The Dhafra Air Base Strikes

The catalyst for this shift was a series of devastating blows to U.S. aerial intelligence networks. In a single 24-hour window, Iranian air defenses successfully intercepted and downed 13 U.S. MQ-9 Reaper surveillance drones. These high-altitude assets are crucial for identifying targets, mapping radar positions, and providing real-time data to U.S. and Israeli strike aircraft.

By neutralizing these drones, Iran has effectively blinded U.S. tactical command. The loss of these assets forced Washington to rethink its reliance on precision air superiority platforms like the F-35 and F-22, which require continuous, detailed target-acquisition data to operate effectively.

The U-2 Hangar Attack: Striking a Cold War Legend

The most shocking escalation, however, took place on the ground at Al Dhafra Air Base in the United Arab Emirates. A precision strike successfully targeted and burned a U.S. U-2 spy plane while it was stored inside its maintenance hangar. The U-2, a legendary Cold War reconnaissance aircraft recently upgraded with modern electro-optical sensors, was destroyed before it could take off.

With a maximum range of 5,600 km and a top speed of 821 km/h, the U-2 was a key pillar of U.S. strategic intelligence. Striking this platform inside a supposedly secure hangar at Al Dhafra exposed the vulnerability of U.S. logistics and marked a qualitative shift in Iran's ability to interdict U.S. intelligence capabilities at their source.

Transitioning to Phase Two: The Heavy Bomber Campaign

Faced with a heavily degraded target-acquisition network, the U.S. President has authorized "Phase Two" of the campaign: a heavy bomber offensive. To execute this, the U.S. Air Force has deployed B-1B Lancer heavy bombers to RAF Fairford in the United Kingdom.

Without detailed, real-time target data, the U.S. is moving away from surgical, small-scale precision strikes. Instead, the strategy relies on the overwhelming payload capacity of strategic bombers to saturate target areas and dismantle Iranian military infrastructure through sheer volume of fire. This shift represents a transition to a much more destructive and unpredictable phase of the conflict.

Airborne Command: E-6B Mercury and E-4B Nightwatch

Because ground-based command and control centers are vulnerable to missile strikes and local intelligence is blinded, the U.S. has moved its operational command entirely into the air. The campaign is being coordinated by E-6B Mercury communications planes (often called "doomsday planes") and the E-4B Nightwatch, which serves as the National Airborne Operations Center.

This airborne command structure was only made possible through a direct, highly sensitive agreement with the United Kingdom. While London officially limits its role to defensive operations in the Middle East, it is actively providing critical logistical, electronic warfare, and radar intelligence support to coordinate the B-1B Lancer strikes from Fairford.

The Geopolitical Quarantine of the Persian Gulf

The strikes on Al Dhafra have triggered severe diplomatic anxiety among the Gulf states. Iran has issued a clear warning: any regional base utilized by the U.S. for offensive or intelligence operations against Iranian territory will become a legitimate target for immediate retaliation.

This threat has effectively initiated a quarantine of the Persian Gulf. Leaders like Iran's President Pezeshkian are successfully pressuring Gulf governments to freeze U.S. military activity. This mirrors the positions of Turkey and Azerbaijan, both of which have frozen all joint military operations and logistical support for the U.S. military to protect their own security.

The Battle to Keep Al Dhafra Online

With Kuwait's Ali Al Salem Air Base already heavily disabled by prior strikes, Al Dhafra in the UAE remains the final operational hub for U.S. drone maintenance and storage. The U-2 is currently deploying every available air defense asset—including South Korean-manufactured interceptor networks—to shield the base from further strikes.

Washington’s goal is to keep Al Dhafra functional until the arrival of the third aircraft carrier, the USS George H.W. Bush (CVN-77), which will join the USS Gerald R. Ford and USS Abraham Lincoln. Carrier movements reflect this high-threat environment: the USS Abraham Lincoln has been observed retreating to a safe distance of 1,000 km, occasionally advancing to 300 km for operations, and immediately returning to deep waters to avoid hypersonic missile range.

Conclusion: The New Limits of U.S. Power

The destruction of the U-2 spy plane and the massive loss of MQ-9 Reaper drones have exposed the structural limits of U.S. military dominance in the region. Without absolute air and intelligence supremacy, Washington is forced to rely on heavy bomber saturation, raising the risk of widespread regional devastation.

As Gulf states move to distance themselves from the U.S. military apparatus to avoid retaliatory strikes, the geopolitical map of the Middle East is being redrawn. The coming weeks will determine whether the arrival of the USS George H.W. Bush can restore U.S. dominance, or if the quarantine of the Gulf has already become a permanent reality.

item.title: Dire Cost of War: US & Israeli Forces Face Ambushes
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Analyzing the heavy toll on U.S. forces at Al Dhafra (221 casualties) and the failed Israeli commando raid in Lebanon targeting a Radwan commander.
item.content:encoded:
High Cost of War: US and Israeli Forces Face Ambushes

The regional war between U.S.-Israeli forces and the Axis of Resistance has entered a highly lethal phase, extracting a severe human cost. In the Persian Gulf, a series of retaliatory strikes has resulted in 221 U.S. casualties, highlighting the vulnerability of forward bases. Simultaneously, on the northern front, a complex Israeli heliborne commando raid in Lebanon has ended in a complete tactical disaster, resulting in the capture of Israeli soldiers by Hezbollah's elite Radwan Force.

The Human Cost: 221 U.S. Casualties in the Gulf

According to official statements released by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), recent retaliatory operations have inflicted significant losses on U.S. forces. Specifically, 21 U.S. Navy personnel associated with the Fifth Fleet were killed or wounded in the Gulf waters.

More alarmingly, a massive strike targeting the U.S. Al Dhafra Air Base in the United Arab Emirates resulted in the injury or death of 200 U.S. military personnel. This brings the total U.S. casualty bill to 221. These numbers represent a dramatic spike in the human cost of U.S. presence, forcing the White House to confront the reality of its exposed regional footprint.

Trump’s Miscalculation: Surrender vs. Retaliation

This sudden escalation was triggered by a severe diplomatic miscalculation by Donald Trump. Iranian President Pezeshkian had previously proposed a conditional neutrality: Iran would not target Gulf Arab states as long as their bases were not used by the U.S. to launch strikes against Iranian territory.

Trump publicly interpreted this proposal as a sign of Iranian "surrender" to the Gulf states under the weight of U.S. heavy bomber deployments. Consequently, Trump declared that U.S. forces would continue conducting offensive operations from these bases. Fearing a complete encirclement, Iran immediately enforced its condition, launching massive strikes against Al Dhafra to prove that no host base is immune from retaliation.

The Weapon Stockpile Monopoly: Rubio’s Ultimatum

The strikes on Al Dhafra have highlighted the sovereignty limits of Gulf host nations. Although these states spend billions of dollars purchasing U.S. weapons and ammunition, they have no physical access to the stockpiles stored inside U.S.-controlled bases. The U.S. military maintains strict physical monopoly over these weapon depots.

This dynamic was laid bare by Senator Marco Rubio, who publicly advocated for bypassing standard legal procedures to immediately transfer Gulf-owned ammunition and weapons directly to Israel for its campaign in Lebanon. This proposal has caused deep outrage in Gulf capitals, exposing that their multi-billion-dollar purchases are functionally treated as U.S. strategic assets to be redistributed at Washington's will.

The Failed Insertion: Ambush in Nabi Chit

On the northern front, Israeli forces suffered a severe tactical setback during a high-risk heliborne operation. Three Israeli helicopters crossed the Syrian-Lebanese border, attempting to land commandos in the mountainous region of Nabi Chit in the eastern Bekaa Valley.

However, Hezbollah’s elite Radwan Force had anticipated the insertion path. Having established a sophisticated multi-layered ambush, Radwan commandos engaged the landing zone with heavy machine guns and anti-aircraft weapons. The ambush completely disrupted the helicopter landing, resulting in intense close-quarters combat on the ground and leading to the capture of several Israeli commandos by Hezbollah forces.

The Ron Arad Cover Story and Radwan Targets

To justify the high-risk operation, Israeli military sources initially claimed the commandos were searching for the remains of Ron Arad, an Israeli Air Force navigator missing since 1986. This explanation was quickly dismissed as a political cover story. Even Arad’s wife publicly criticized the raid, stating that there was no logical reason to sacrifice the lives of living soldiers to retrieve the bones of the dead.

Investigative analysis reveals that the true objective of the raid was the abduction of a high-ranking Radwan Force commander to secure tactical intelligence. The failure of this capture operation resulted in heavy casualties, including the wounding of the son of Israel’s Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, who was reportedly part of the elite unit.

Heavy Clashes in Khiam: The Ground Defense

Simultaneously, the ground front in the town of Khiam in southern Lebanon has turned into a war of attrition. Israeli units attempting to advance were met with fierce resistance. Hezbollah fighters engaged Israeli armor and infantry using medium weapons and anti-tank guided missiles (ATGMs).

The battle for Khiam has shown that despite weeks of heavy U.S.-led air campaigns, Hezbollah’s tactical defensive lines remain intact. Israeli military commentators have admitted that the ground combat is extremely harsh and unforgiving, warning that the dense network of ambushes makes any rapid advance highly costly.

Conclusion: The Cost of Strategic Hubris

The events of the past 24 hours have demonstrated the high cost of military and diplomatic hubris. Trump’s misinterpretation of Iranian diplomatic initiatives led directly to the Al Dhafra strikes and 221 U.S. casualties. Meanwhile, Netanyahu’s push for high-profile commando raids in Lebanon has resulted in captured soldiers and tactical defeats.

As both the U.S. and Israel find themselves caught in multiple ambushes—both on the ground in Lebanon and in the military installations of the Gulf—the limits of their military options are becoming clear. Without a diplomatic exit, the human cost will continue to climb, threatening to destabilize the entire region.

item.title: Ali Al Salem Struck: Iran's Heavy Missiles in Kuwait
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Iranian heavy ballistic missiles destroy the runway at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait, cutting US air operations by 50%.
item.content:encoded:
Ali Al Salem Struck: Iran's Heavy Missiles in Kuwait

For the first time in this conflict, Iran has transitioned from standard ballistic missile strikes to heavy ballistic missile bombardment, and the target was the nerve center of American air power in the Gulf: Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait. The strike destroyed one of the base's two runways, immediately cutting US air operations capacity by 50% and marking a qualitative escalation that redefines the operational calculus for the entire theater.

This is not a harassing strike. This is a deliberate attempt to permanently remove Ali Al Salem from the order of battle.

The Strike: From Ballistic to Heavy Ballistic

The Iranian attack on Ali Al Salem represents a fundamental escalation in weapons employment. Prior strikes against American installations in the Gulf used standard ballistic missiles and drone swarms—weapons designed to damage equipment, disable radars, and degrade electronic systems. The logic was disruption, not destruction.

That logic has now been abandoned. The IRGC deployed heavy ballistic missiles against Ali Al Salem with a single objective: destroy the physical infrastructure that makes the base operational. The primary target was the runway complex itself.

Ali Al Salem sits 144 meters above sea level and features two asphalt-and-concrete runways. The primary runway measures approximately 2,989 meters by 45 meters—a standard configuration for high-performance military aircraft operations. The strike destroyed this runway, reducing the base's operational capacity by half in a single salvo.

The second runway remains intact, but the precedent has been set. A follow-up strike targeting the remaining runway would take Ali Al Salem entirely offline. The base now operates in a precarious cycle: partial operations on the surviving runway, under the constant threat of a second strike that would deliver a complete shutdown.

Why Ali Al Salem Matters: The Hub of American Air Power

Ali Al Salem is not merely another American installation in the Gulf. It is the principal center of US Air Force operations in the region, and its destruction would represent the single most consequential blow to American force projection capability since the conflict began.

The base serves as the permanent home of the 386th Air Expeditionary Wing, which functions as:

  • The primary air transit hub and gateway for combat support to Joint and Coalition forces.
  • The main staging point for reconnaissance and surveillance operations across the theater.
  • The coordination center for combat air support, medical evacuation, and combat search and rescue (CSAR).

Under the 386th AEW umbrella, several critical groups operate from Ali Al Salem:

  • 386th Expeditionary Reconnaissance Group: Aerial intelligence collection.
  • 387th Expeditionary Reconnaissance Group: Extended surveillance operations.
  • 407th Expeditionary Reconnaissance Group: Specialized reconnaissance missions.

Additionally, the Ninth Air Force maintains its effective headquarters at Ali Al Salem, making the base the command node for all US Air Force operations in the Central Command area of responsibility.

The MQ-9 Reaper Factor

Perhaps the most strategically significant aspect of Ali Al Salem's operational profile is its role as the primary launch point for MQ-9 Reaper unmanned aerial vehicles. The MQ-9s that operate over Iranian airspace—conducting surveillance, target acquisition, and strike missions—originate from Kuwait.

This means that the drones being shot down over Iran, or conducting strike operations against Iranian targets, are overwhelmingly launching from Ali Al Salem. By striking the base's runway infrastructure, Iran is attacking the source of the drone operations that are directly supporting the bombing campaign against its territory.

The logic is direct and symmetrical: if the United States uses Kuwait-based drones to support strikes on Iranian missile cities, Iran will destroy the bases from which those drones operate.

13,500 American Troops: The Heaviest Footprint

Kuwait hosts the largest concentration of American military personnel in the Gulf theater. As of the current campaign, approximately 13,500 US troops are stationed in Kuwait across multiple installations:

Installation Primary Function
Ali Al Salem Air Base Main USAF operations hub, 386th AEW headquarters
Camp Arifjan US Army installation with Air Force support units
Ahmad Al Jaber Air Base Secondary air base hosting US air units and equipment

This concentration of forces is a legacy of the 1991 Gulf War and the subsequent long-term strategic defense cooperation agreement between Kuwait and the United States. Since Operation Desert Storm, Kuwait has served as the primary staging ground for American military operations in the region—a role that has now made it the most exposed American position in the current conflict.

More American soldiers have been killed and wounded in Kuwait than in any other Gulf state during this campaign. The heavy troop presence, combined with the forward-deployed nature of the installations, makes Kuwait the epicenter of American vulnerability.

The Strategic Defense Partnership: Since 1991

The US-Kuwait defense relationship is the deepest and most institutionally embedded partnership in the Gulf. Under the Long-Term Strategic Defense Cooperation Agreement, Kuwaiti bases have been integrated into American force structure to a degree unmatched by any other GCC state.

This integration was designed for power projection—enabling the United States to rapidly deploy and sustain forces across the Middle East. In the current crisis, however, that deep integration has become a strategic liability. The bases were configured for offensive operations against regional adversaries, not for defense against a state-level ballistic missile campaign directed at their permanent infrastructure.

The air defense systems protecting Kuwaiti installations were designed to handle shorter-range threats—rockets, mortars, and cruise missiles. Heavy ballistic missiles carrying warheads exceeding one ton present a threat category that the existing defensive architecture was not built to counter.

The Repair-and-Strike Cycle

The destruction of one runway at Ali Al Salem creates a tactical dilemma that extends far beyond the immediate operational disruption. The base now faces what military planners call a "repair-and-strike cycle"—a pattern where damaged infrastructure is repaired, only to be struck again before full operations can resume.

This cycle is extraordinarily resource-intensive for the defending side:

  • Runway repair requires specialized engineering teams, materials, and heavy equipment—all of which must be brought in under the threat of follow-up strikes.
  • Force protection demands that defensive assets be concentrated around repair operations, drawing resources away from other installations.
  • Operational tempo drops precipitously as commanders must plan around uncertain runway availability.

For the attacking side, the cycle is far less costly. A single heavy ballistic missile salvo can undo days or weeks of repair work in minutes. The attacker maintains the initiative, choosing when and where to strike, while the defender is locked into a reactive posture.

The Heavy Bomber vs. Heavy Missile Equation

The escalation at Ali Al Salem crystallizes a symmetry that defines Phase 2 of the conflict: heavy bombers against heavy missiles.

The United States has deployed its most capable strategic bombers—the B-2 Spirit, B-52 Stratofortress, and B-21 Raider—to strike Iranian targets with massive ordnance. Iran has responded with its heaviest ballistic missiles to strike the bases from which those bomber operations are supported.

This creates a direct exchange ratio that neither side can sustain indefinitely:

  • Every B-2 sortie against an Iranian missile city requires functional runways, fuel depots, and maintenance facilities at Gulf bases.
  • Every Iranian heavy missile strike against those bases degrades the ability to generate the next B-2 sortie.
  • The cost asymmetry favors the missile: a heavy ballistic missile costs a fraction of the infrastructure it destroys, while repairing a runway costs far more than the missile that cratered it.

The 50% Reduction and What Comes Next

The immediate impact of the Ali Al Salem strike is quantifiable: a 50% reduction in air operations capacity. With one runway destroyed and one remaining, the base can continue limited operations—but at half capacity, with degraded surge capability, and under the perpetual threat of a second strike.

The implications cascade through the entire theater:

  • MQ-9 Reaper sorties over Iran are reduced.
  • Air transit capacity for personnel and equipment is halved.
  • Combat search and rescue response times increase.
  • Medical evacuation capability is degraded.
  • Reconnaissance flight schedules are compressed.

If the second runway is struck, Ali Al Salem goes completely dark. The 386th Air Expeditionary Wing would need to relocate—an operation measured in weeks, not hours—and the alternative basing options in the Gulf are themselves under missile threat.

Conclusion: The Base That Cannot Fall

Ali Al Salem Air Base is the single most important American air installation in the Gulf theater. Its partial disabling represents a strategic achievement for the IRGC and a crisis for US Central Command. The transition from standard ballistic strikes to heavy missile bombardment signals that Iran has committed to a destruction doctrine—not disruption, not degradation, but the physical elimination of American basing infrastructure.

The 50% capacity reduction is the beginning, not the end. The repair-and-strike cycle ensures that Ali Al Salem will operate in a degraded state for the foreseeable future, and the 13,500 American troops in Kuwait now face the reality that their primary operational hub is no longer secure.

The heavy bomber versus heavy missile equation has arrived at its logical conclusion: neither side can project force without absorbing punishing retaliatory strikes against the infrastructure that enables that projection.
item.yandex:full-text:
Ali Al Salem Struck: Iran's Heavy Missiles in Kuwait

For the first time in this conflict, Iran has transitioned from standard ballistic missile strikes to heavy ballistic missile bombardment, and the target was the nerve center of American air power in the Gulf: Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait. The strike destroyed one of the base's two runways, immediately cutting US air operations capacity by 50% and marking a qualitative escalation that redefines the operational calculus for the entire theater.

This is not a harassing strike. This is a deliberate attempt to permanently remove Ali Al Salem from the order of battle.

The Strike: From Ballistic to Heavy Ballistic

The Iranian attack on Ali Al Salem represents a fundamental escalation in weapons employment. Prior strikes against American installations in the Gulf used standard ballistic missiles and drone swarms—weapons designed to damage equipment, disable radars, and degrade electronic systems. The logic was disruption, not destruction.

That logic has now been abandoned. The IRGC deployed heavy ballistic missiles against Ali Al Salem with a single objective: destroy the physical infrastructure that makes the base operational. The primary target was the runway complex itself.

Ali Al Salem sits 144 meters above sea level and features two asphalt-and-concrete runways. The primary runway measures approximately 2,989 meters by 45 meters—a standard configuration for high-performance military aircraft operations. The strike destroyed this runway, reducing the base's operational capacity by half in a single salvo.

The second runway remains intact, but the precedent has been set. A follow-up strike targeting the remaining runway would take Ali Al Salem entirely offline. The base now operates in a precarious cycle: partial operations on the surviving runway, under the constant threat of a second strike that would deliver a complete shutdown.

Why Ali Al Salem Matters: The Hub of American Air Power

Ali Al Salem is not merely another American installation in the Gulf. It is the principal center of US Air Force operations in the region, and its destruction would represent the single most consequential blow to American force projection capability since the conflict began.

The base serves as the permanent home of the 386th Air Expeditionary Wing, which functions as:

  • The primary air transit hub and gateway for combat support to Joint and Coalition forces.
  • The main staging point for reconnaissance and surveillance operations across the theater.
  • The coordination center for combat air support, medical evacuation, and combat search and rescue (CSAR).

Under the 386th AEW umbrella, several critical groups operate from Ali Al Salem:

  • 386th Expeditionary Reconnaissance Group: Aerial intelligence collection.
  • 387th Expeditionary Reconnaissance Group: Extended surveillance operations.
  • 407th Expeditionary Reconnaissance Group: Specialized reconnaissance missions.

Additionally, the Ninth Air Force maintains its effective headquarters at Ali Al Salem, making the base the command node for all US Air Force operations in the Central Command area of responsibility.

The MQ-9 Reaper Factor

Perhaps the most strategically significant aspect of Ali Al Salem's operational profile is its role as the primary launch point for MQ-9 Reaper unmanned aerial vehicles. The MQ-9s that operate over Iranian airspace—conducting surveillance, target acquisition, and strike missions—originate from Kuwait.

This means that the drones being shot down over Iran, or conducting strike operations against Iranian targets, are overwhelmingly launching from Ali Al Salem. By striking the base's runway infrastructure, Iran is attacking the source of the drone operations that are directly supporting the bombing campaign against its territory.

The logic is direct and symmetrical: if the United States uses Kuwait-based drones to support strikes on Iranian missile cities, Iran will destroy the bases from which those drones operate.

13,500 American Troops: The Heaviest Footprint

Kuwait hosts the largest concentration of American military personnel in the Gulf theater. As of the current campaign, approximately 13,500 US troops are stationed in Kuwait across multiple installations:

Installation Primary Function
Ali Al Salem Air Base Main USAF operations hub, 386th AEW headquarters
Camp Arifjan US Army installation with Air Force support units
Ahmad Al Jaber Air Base Secondary air base hosting US air units and equipment

This concentration of forces is a legacy of the 1991 Gulf War and the subsequent long-term strategic defense cooperation agreement between Kuwait and the United States. Since Operation Desert Storm, Kuwait has served as the primary staging ground for American military operations in the region—a role that has now made it the most exposed American position in the current conflict.

More American soldiers have been killed and wounded in Kuwait than in any other Gulf state during this campaign. The heavy troop presence, combined with the forward-deployed nature of the installations, makes Kuwait the epicenter of American vulnerability.

The Strategic Defense Partnership: Since 1991

The US-Kuwait defense relationship is the deepest and most institutionally embedded partnership in the Gulf. Under the Long-Term Strategic Defense Cooperation Agreement, Kuwaiti bases have been integrated into American force structure to a degree unmatched by any other GCC state.

This integration was designed for power projection—enabling the United States to rapidly deploy and sustain forces across the Middle East. In the current crisis, however, that deep integration has become a strategic liability. The bases were configured for offensive operations against regional adversaries, not for defense against a state-level ballistic missile campaign directed at their permanent infrastructure.

The air defense systems protecting Kuwaiti installations were designed to handle shorter-range threats—rockets, mortars, and cruise missiles. Heavy ballistic missiles carrying warheads exceeding one ton present a threat category that the existing defensive architecture was not built to counter.

The Repair-and-Strike Cycle

The destruction of one runway at Ali Al Salem creates a tactical dilemma that extends far beyond the immediate operational disruption. The base now faces what military planners call a "repair-and-strike cycle"—a pattern where damaged infrastructure is repaired, only to be struck again before full operations can resume.

This cycle is extraordinarily resource-intensive for the defending side:

  • Runway repair requires specialized engineering teams, materials, and heavy equipment—all of which must be brought in under the threat of follow-up strikes.
  • Force protection demands that defensive assets be concentrated around repair operations, drawing resources away from other installations.
  • Operational tempo drops precipitously as commanders must plan around uncertain runway availability.

For the attacking side, the cycle is far less costly. A single heavy ballistic missile salvo can undo days or weeks of repair work in minutes. The attacker maintains the initiative, choosing when and where to strike, while the defender is locked into a reactive posture.

The Heavy Bomber vs. Heavy Missile Equation

The escalation at Ali Al Salem crystallizes a symmetry that defines Phase 2 of the conflict: heavy bombers against heavy missiles.

The United States has deployed its most capable strategic bombers—the B-2 Spirit, B-52 Stratofortress, and B-21 Raider—to strike Iranian targets with massive ordnance. Iran has responded with its heaviest ballistic missiles to strike the bases from which those bomber operations are supported.

This creates a direct exchange ratio that neither side can sustain indefinitely:

  • Every B-2 sortie against an Iranian missile city requires functional runways, fuel depots, and maintenance facilities at Gulf bases.
  • Every Iranian heavy missile strike against those bases degrades the ability to generate the next B-2 sortie.
  • The cost asymmetry favors the missile: a heavy ballistic missile costs a fraction of the infrastructure it destroys, while repairing a runway costs far more than the missile that cratered it.

The 50% Reduction and What Comes Next

The immediate impact of the Ali Al Salem strike is quantifiable: a 50% reduction in air operations capacity. With one runway destroyed and one remaining, the base can continue limited operations—but at half capacity, with degraded surge capability, and under the perpetual threat of a second strike.

The implications cascade through the entire theater:

  • MQ-9 Reaper sorties over Iran are reduced.
  • Air transit capacity for personnel and equipment is halved.
  • Combat search and rescue response times increase.
  • Medical evacuation capability is degraded.
  • Reconnaissance flight schedules are compressed.

If the second runway is struck, Ali Al Salem goes completely dark. The 386th Air Expeditionary Wing would need to relocate—an operation measured in weeks, not hours—and the alternative basing options in the Gulf are themselves under missile threat.

Conclusion: The Base That Cannot Fall

Ali Al Salem Air Base is the single most important American air installation in the Gulf theater. Its partial disabling represents a strategic achievement for the IRGC and a crisis for US Central Command. The transition from standard ballistic strikes to heavy missile bombardment signals that Iran has committed to a destruction doctrine—not disruption, not degradation, but the physical elimination of American basing infrastructure.

The 50% capacity reduction is the beginning, not the end. The repair-and-strike cycle ensures that Ali Al Salem will operate in a degraded state for the foreseeable future, and the 13,500 American troops in Kuwait now face the reality that their primary operational hub is no longer secure.

The heavy bomber versus heavy missile equation has arrived at its logical conclusion: neither side can project force without absorbing punishing retaliatory strikes against the infrastructure that enables that projection.

item.title: Araghchi: Plan B Will Fail Like Plan A Did
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Iran's Araghchi warns Israel's Phase 2 nuclear strikes will fail. With 42% of missiles intact and Khorramshahr targeting Dimona, the calculus shifts.
item.content:encoded:
Araghchi: Plan B Will Fail Like Plan A Did

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has delivered one of the most direct and consequential strategic messages of this crisis. Speaking in language that directly mirrors the terminology used by Israeli and American military planners, Araghchi declared: "Just as you failed in Plan A, you will fail in Plan B." This is not rhetorical posturing. It is a calculated response to the operational realities now unfolding across the theater.

The Collapse of Plan A: The "Clean and Swift" Illusion

Israel's initial strategic concept—Plan A—was built on the premise of a rapid, surgical air campaign designed to neutralize Iran's missile infrastructure before Tehran could mount a meaningful response. The logic was straightforward: deploy B-2 Spirit stealth bombers and B-52 Stratofortresses to strike hardened mountain tunnel complexes, seal the entrances and exits identified by satellite reconnaissance, and bury Iran's ballistic arsenal underground.

The results on the ground tell a different story. While the United States claims to have neutralized approximately 58% of Iran's missile inventory, the operational reality is far more complex. The strikes succeeded in sealing many of the tunnel entrances and exits across Iran's mountain-based missile cities. However, the missiles themselves remain largely intact inside those mountains. The infrastructure is damaged; the weapons are not destroyed.

More critically, Iran has executed a decisive tactical pivot that fundamentally undermines the assumptions behind Plan A: the transition from liquid-fueled to solid-fueled ballistic missiles. Solid-fuel missiles do not require the lengthy pre-launch fueling procedures that make liquid-fueled systems vulnerable to preemptive strikes. They can be launched from mobile platforms with minimal preparation time, making them extraordinarily difficult to detect and intercept from the air.

Plan B: The Nuclear Facilities Gamble

With Plan A's failure to deliver a clean decapitation of Iran's missile force, Israel and its American partners are now reportedly pivoting to Phase 2—what Araghchi explicitly calls "Plan B." This phase centers on striking Iran's nuclear enrichment facilities, particularly Fordow and Isfahan.

The strategic logic behind this shift is twofold. First, Israeli leaders argue that destroying Iran's nuclear infrastructure would force the IRGC into a position of capitulation, as it would eliminate Tehran's ultimate strategic deterrent. Second, the Israeli political establishment—voiced openly by the Prime Minister in the Knesset—has made clear that President Trump's direct military intervention was designed specifically to prevent Israel from deploying its own nuclear weapons against Iran.

This reveals a critical dynamic: the American intervention is not purely about supporting Israel. It is about controlling Israel's nuclear escalation threshold. By offering conventional strikes on Iranian nuclear sites, Washington is attempting to remove the justification for an Israeli nuclear first strike.

The E-6B Mercury Deployment: Nuclear Command Airborne

The deployment of the E-6B Mercury—the United States' airborne nuclear command and control platform, sometimes referred to as the "Doomsday Plane"—to the Middle East theater is perhaps the most alarming indicator of where this escalation is heading.

The E-6B serves as an airborne relay for nuclear launch commands. Its presence in the region signals that Washington is preparing for scenarios that go well beyond conventional strikes. The aircraft's deployment, combined with the Boeing 707-based Tacamo platform's operational posture, indicates that the United States is establishing a complete airborne command architecture capable of directing strategic strikes, including submarine-launched ballistic missiles, as part of the contingency planning.

This is not a routine deployment. It is an operational signal that the nuclear threshold is being actively managed, not merely discussed.

The Khorramshahr Equation: Iran's Counter-Deterrent

Araghchi's confidence in declaring Plan B's inevitable failure rests on a concrete military reality: Iran's Khorramshahr ballistic missile.

The Khorramshahr has already demonstrated its operational capability during the current conflict by striking Tel Aviv with devastating effect. Iran's message is unambiguous: if Israel strikes Iran's nuclear facilities, the Khorramshahr will be directed at Dimona—Israel's own nuclear reactor complex in the Negev Desert. The logic is one of symmetrical escalation: whatever damage Israel inflicts on Fordow and Isfahan, Iran will inflict equivalent or greater damage on Dimona.

This creates an intolerable strategic paradox for Israeli planners. Striking Iran's nuclear infrastructure does not eliminate the retaliatory threat—it guarantees it. And the retaliatory target would be Israel's most sensitive and symbolically important nuclear installation.

Iran's three-pronged deterrent message is clear:

  1. Khorramshahr to Dimona: A direct nuclear facility-for-nuclear facility retaliatory doctrine.
  2. Hadid-110 drone swarms: Expanded autonomous strike capability against naval assets, including carrier groups.
  3. Naval mine warfare: Intensified mining operations targeting carrier strike groups and supply lines through the Strait of Hormuz.

The 42% Problem: What Remains Is Enough

According to the Pentagon's own assessments—cited by the Trump administration—approximately 42% of Iran's ballistic missile inventory remains operational. While American officials have attempted to frame this as a diminished threat, suggesting the remaining arsenal is insufficient to alter the strategic balance, Araghchi's response directly challenges this calculation.

The 42% figure represents hundreds of missiles, including the Khorramshahr variants capable of carrying warheads heavy enough to cause catastrophic damage to hardened targets. Iran does not need 100% of its arsenal to execute a devastating retaliatory strike. It needs a fraction of what remains—and it has far more than a fraction.

Israel's Economic Clock: $4.5 Billion Per Day

The urgency behind Israel's push toward Plan B is not purely military—it is existential economics. According to Israeli government figures, the current conflict is costing the Israeli economy approximately $3.7 billion per day in direct economic losses, plus an additional $1 billion in daily defense ministry expenditures. This brings the total daily hemorrhage to roughly $4.5 billion.

At this burn rate, Israeli officials have privately acknowledged that the country cannot sustain full-scale military operations beyond Saturday. The 24-to-48-hour window for transitioning to Phase 2 is not a strategic preference—it is a financial deadline.

This economic pressure is pushing Israeli decision-makers toward increasingly desperate options, including what they term "limited nuclear use" or, at minimum, a comprehensive conventional strike campaign against Iran's nuclear infrastructure to force a rapid conclusion to hostilities.

The Radiological Calculation: UF6 and Chemical Risk

Israeli military planners have attempted to downplay the environmental consequences of strikes on uranium enrichment facilities. Their argument centers on the claim that the primary risk from attacking facilities like Fordow and Isfahan would be chemical rather than radiological.

The technical basis for this assessment is that uranium hexafluoride (UF6)—the compound used in centrifuge enrichment—decomposes into toxic chemical agents upon exposure to air, but does not necessarily produce widespread radioactive contamination. Israeli experts argue that because Iran's nuclear program remains in the early stages of the fuel cycle, the radiological risks are manageable.

However, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has expressed concerns that go beyond the early-stage fuel cycle assessment. The United States itself has voiced environmental anxieties about potential radiological leakage following strikes on Iranian nuclear sites—a position that creates friction between Washington's stated objectives and Israel's operational planning.

Conclusion: Strategy Against Strategy

Araghchi's declaration that Plan B will fail just as Plan A did is not bluster. It is anchored in the operational mathematics of the conflict:

  • Iran retains sufficient missile capability (42% by Pentagon estimates) to execute devastating retaliatory strikes.
  • The Khorramshahr missile provides a direct, symmetrical deterrent against Israeli nuclear facilities.
  • Israel's economic hemorrhage of $4.5 billion per day creates an unsustainable timeline.
  • The deployment of the E-6B Mercury signals nuclear-level contingency planning.
  • Strikes on enrichment facilities carry chemical and potential radiological consequences that complicate the political calculus.

The transition from Plan A to Plan B does not resolve the fundamental problem. It merely shifts the arena of failure from missile suppression to nuclear brinkmanship—a domain where the consequences of miscalculation are orders of magnitude more severe.

item.title: Phase 2: Iran Shifts to Heavy Missiles on Gulf Bases
item.author: research@khalidnaami.com (Khalid Naami)
item.dc:creator: Khalid Naami
item.description: Iran escalates from drone strikes to heavy ballistic missiles targeting US bases in the Gulf. Ben Gurion and Ramat David hit as Phase 2 reshapes the war.
item.content:encoded:
Phase 2: Iran Shifts to Heavy Missiles on Gulf Bases

The conflict has entered a fundamentally different operational phase. What the American side designates as "Phase 2" involves expanded B-52, B-2 Spirit, and B-21 Raider strikes against Iran's strategic missile launch sites and underground cities. But the Iranian response has escalated in equal measure—and in a direction that Washington and Tel Aviv did not anticipate.

Iran has shifted from targeting radars, electronic warfare systems, and logistical support infrastructure to destroying the physical infrastructure of American and Israeli military bases across the entire Gulf region using heavy ballistic missiles. The rules of engagement have changed completely.

The American Phased Campaign: From Missiles to Nuclear Infrastructure

The original American operational plan was structured in sequential phases. Phase 1 focused on neutralizing Iran's ballistic missile capability through strikes on mountain-based missile cities using B-2 Spirit and B-52 Stratofortress sorties. Phase 2, as initially conceived, was meant to shift toward destroying Iran's nuclear enrichment facilities and missile manufacturing plants.

However, the operational timeline has been compressed and resequenced. What was originally planned as Phase 2—striking nuclear infrastructure—has now been pushed to Phase 3. The current Phase 2 has been redefined as an expanded bombardment campaign targeting the strategic launch infrastructure that survived the initial wave, using the full spectrum of American strategic bombers including the B-21 Raider.

The American objective remains unchanged: force the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to lay down its arms. President Trump has publicly called on the IRGC to surrender. The escalation to Phase 2 is designed to make that demand unavoidable by eliminating Iran's ability to project force.

Iran's Tactical Pivot: From Drones to Destruction

In Phase 1, Iran's retaliatory strikes were deliberately calibrated. The IRGC targeted radars, electronic warfare nodes, and digital logistics systems supporting American operations—the auxiliary infrastructure that enables combat operations without striking the physical bases themselves. The intent was to degrade operational capability while preserving a degree of escalation management.

Phase 2 has changed that calculus entirely. Following the American declaration that "the initiative is in America's hands" and the direct escalation by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, the IRGC's response has been symmetrical: if the United States escalates to destroying Iran's core infrastructure, Iran will destroy the core infrastructure of American bases.

The shift is concrete and measurable:

  • From drones to heavy ballistic missiles: Khorramshahr-4, Kheibar, and Fattah hypersonic missiles are now being directed at US military installations.
  • From degradation to destruction: The target set has shifted from radar dishes and electronic systems to runways, hangars, command centers, and fuel storage—the permanent infrastructure that defines a base's existence.
  • Unified target bank: US bases in the Gulf and Israeli military installations are now treated as a single, integrated target set. Ramat David Air Base, Al-Udeid in Qatar, and bases in Kuwait and Bahrain are all on the same target list.

Ben Gurion Airport: The Strategic Chokepoint

One of the most consequential strikes in Phase 2 has been directed at Ben Gurion International Airport. The targeting logic is both military and strategic: Ben Gurion's military wing serves as a critical logistics hub for the Israeli Air Force, and the airport itself is the only viable node for large-scale evacuation operations.

According to Israeli sources, over 2,000 residents have already been evacuated from Tel Aviv alone, with the number expected to grow. Approximately 5,000 Israeli nationals who had gathered in the UAE were preparing for an air bridge back to Israel via Ben Gurion. The strikes on the airport have disrupted this evacuation corridor, forcing a rerouting of operations.

The IRGC's intent is clear: take Ben Gurion's military wing permanently offline, exactly as Ramat David Air Base has been targeted for the same purpose. If both installations are rendered inoperable, Israel's capacity to sustain air operations and manage civilian evacuations simultaneously becomes severely constrained.

The Gulf States' Financial and Strategic Trap

The economic dimension of Phase 2 is as critical as the military one. The United States has effectively demanded that Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states finance the war effort. This decision shifts the financial burden from the already-strained American and Israeli defense budgets onto Gulf economies that are themselves under severe pressure.

The financial arithmetic is devastating:

  • Israel's daily losses: Approximately $3.7 billion in economic shutdown costs plus $1 billion in direct defense expenditures—totaling roughly $4.5 billion per day.
  • Israel's defense allocation: $3 billion was transferred to the Ministry of Defense on the first day of operations, but this covers only the initial phase.
  • Gulf reserves window: The UAE, Bahrain, and Qatar have between 12 and 22 days of surplus reserves from the preceding production period. Beyond that window, these states face their own financial crisis.
  • American daily costs: Approximately $900 million to $1 billion per day for the sustained bombing campaign.

The economic clock is ticking for every party in the coalition. The longer the conflict continues, the more unsustainable the financing becomes—and Iran's strategy of graduated escalation is designed precisely to exploit this vulnerability.

Qatar's Al-Udeid Dilemma

Al-Udeid Air Base in Qatar remains one of the most critical command and control nodes for American operations in the region. The Qatari authorities face an impossible dilemma: they want to protect the base's physical infrastructure—which represents billions in investment—while that same infrastructure is being used as a primary hub for Phase 2 operations against Iran.

This has created a direct crisis between Doha and Tehran. Iran views Al-Udeid's continued operational role as making Qatar a legitimate combatant in the conflict. The Qatari government argues it is providing only defensive support, but the operational reality—with Al-Udeid serving as a key command center for offensive strikes—makes that distinction increasingly untenable.

Kuwait and Bahrain: Maximum Exposure

Among the Gulf bases, Kuwait and Bahrain are absorbing the heaviest pressure. The American military presence in Kuwait is being subjected to sustained attrition strikes, with large-scale drone swarms preceding the heavy missile waves. Bahrain, home to the US Fifth Fleet headquarters, has already been struck in Phase 1 and now faces infrastructure-level targeting in Phase 2.

The sequential escalation follows a clear pattern:

  1. Initial wave: Drone swarms against Kuwaiti bases to saturate air defenses.
  2. Follow-up: Heavy ballistic missile strikes targeting permanent infrastructure across all Gulf installations.
  3. Sustained pressure: Continued missile salvos designed to prevent repair and reconstitution of damaged facilities.

British, French, and Ukrainian air defense reinforcements deployed to Gulf states have proven insufficient against the new generation of Iranian missiles, which are specifically designed to penetrate layered defense systems.

The Israeli Air Force's Expanding Front

Simultaneously, Israel's air operations are expanding into Lebanon, creating a multi-front resource drain. The campaign has followed a pattern of incremental escalation:

  1. Beirut Embassy: Initial plans to strike near the Iranian diplomatic presence were abandoned.
  2. Southern Suburbs (Dahieh): Direct strikes on Hezbollah infrastructure, framed as targeting IRGC presence.
  3. Bekaa Valley: Expansion of the strike zone deep into Lebanese territory.

Israeli ground forces have suffered casualties in these engagements, with at least eight soldiers reported as having sustained serious to critical injuries. This expanding front diverts resources from the primary campaign against Iran while simultaneously generating additional political and humanitarian complications.

The Attrition Equation: Iran's Strategic Patience

The fundamental miscalculation by American and Israeli planners was the assumption that Iran would launch its entire missile inventory in a single massive salvo of 600-700 missiles, depleting over 50% of its reserves and creating an opportunity for a decisive follow-up strike.

Instead, Iran has adopted a strategy of graduated escalation—methodically increasing the intensity and expanding the target set while preserving its strategic reserves. This approach forces the coalition into a war of attrition that it cannot financially or operationally sustain:

  • Every day costs the coalition approximately $5.5 billion combined.
  • Gulf reserves have a 15-22 day operational window.
  • Iran's missile production capacity continues to operate, partially offsetting combat expenditures.
  • The IRGC explicitly states that "the initiative remains in our hands"—a direct response to the American claim of operational dominance.

Conclusion: Destruction Replaces Degradation

Phase 2 represents a qualitative transformation in the conflict. The Iranian shift from degrading auxiliary systems to destroying permanent base infrastructure signals that the IRGC has abandoned restraint in its targeting doctrine. American bases in the Gulf are no longer being temporarily disabled—they are being systematically destroyed.

The financial burden, the expanding target set, and the graduated escalation strategy create an attrition dynamic that favors the defender. As the coalition burns through approximately $5.5 billion per day with a finite Gulf reserves window, the strategic question is no longer whether Phase 2 will succeed, but how long the coalition can sustain it before the economics force a political resolution.
